subtopic: PROVISION FOR INSPECTION AND STANDARDS OF QUALITY

speakeroldname: Mr. E. F. Whelan (Essex Soufh) moved
subtopic: PROVISION FOR INSPECTION AND STANDARDS OF QUALITY
speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill No. C-130, respecting the inspection of tobacco and tobacco products entering into international and interprovincial trade (tobacco inspection act).

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INSPECTION AND STANDARDS OF QUALITY
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INSPECTION AND STANDARDS OF QUALITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to provide standards of quality for tobacco and tobacco products in the export-import and interprovincial tobacco industry in order to protect the financial interest of the tobacco farmers and the physical health of the consumers. This bill is similar in principle, substance and form to the Meat Inspection Act.
I believe we all realize that for a great many people of the nation the habit of smoking will continue for a long time to come. I believe it is the duty of parliament to make sure that tobacco products used for human consumption, whether manufactured here in Canada or in some other nation, should be made as safe as possible, and should have some form of government inspection. We
know at one time tobacco stems were not used in manufactured tobacco, but in some instances today this is not the case and they are being used to the extent of several million pounds, creating a large tobacco surplus and marketing problem.
This bill gives similar powers to the Minister of Agriculture as does the Meat Inspection Act, in respect of labelling the product so as to identify the ingredients and additives which may be in the manufactured tobacco product. This bill also allows standards to be made from time to time, as prescribed by regulation of the governor in council.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

subtopic: MR. HALES-STATEMENT BY AGRICULTURE MINISTER RESPECTING TURKEY IMPORTS
MR. HALES-STATEMENT BY AGRICULTURE MINISTER RESPECTING TURKEY IMPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to raise a question of privilege concerning the Minister of Agriculture and hon. members of this house. On September 10, in answer to a question posed by the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort-Tisdale, the minister stated, as recorded at page 7826 of Hansard:
In the last two weeks there have been no Importations of turkeys from the United States-
On October 7 a question was posed by the hon. member for Huron, and a supplementary question by the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar, which the minister said he would take as notice. On the following day, October 8, the minister said in part:
During the week ending September 5, 185,892 pounds; week ending September 12, 135,500 pounds: week ending September 19, 83,752 pounds and the week ending September 26, 45,112 pounds, making a total for the month of September of 450,256 pounds, bringing the total imports to that date to 8,214,159 pounds.
The point is that on September 10 we were told that there were no importations in the two weeks covering August 29 to September 5 and September 5 to September 10; then we were later advised there were importations in the poundages I have just quoted. So I think the house was misinformed in this respect. In the same statement the minister also said,

Question of Privilege
as found on page 8870 of Hansard, with reference to the turkey producers and his request for suggestions from them:
As yet I have received no reply.
I have here price information release No. 231 of the Ontario turkey association which contains this statement:
It was agreed the industry still considers import controls are what we need, but short of achieving this the O.T.A. fully endorses the C.T.F.'s efforts to have the government step the live tariff up another 2 cents, to 4 cents per pound, as recommended by the Manitoba association with C.T.F. approval. This request crossed a letter from Mr. Hays a week ago Monday.
That was September 21.
In this, the minister asked for specific data on our tariff position, which the Manitoba brief gave concisely. The next move is up to Mr. Hays.
I know the minister did not want to misrepresent the facts nor did he wish to mislead the house, but I think the record should be kept straight.

speakeroldname: Hon. Harry W. Hays (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: MR. HALES-STATEMENT BY AGRICULTURE MINISTER RESPECTING TURKEY IMPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as you and all hon. members will recall, there was a great deal of turkey talk in the house.
I would not want to mislead hon. members of the house in so far as the turkey situation is concerned. Until I check Hansard I am not admitting that I said there were no importations of turkeys whatsoever in those two weeks although I am not saying I did not say so. But it seems to me that on every occasion I said that imports of turkeys had practically dried up with the exception of one plant where they were still coming in.
I have written three letters to the turkey federation. The letter to which the hon. member for Wellington South has referred was one from the Ontario turkey federation. I have received correspondence from the British Columbia turkey people and the Alberta turkey people, and I have asked them all to get together and send me a resolution from the turkey federation of Canada with the support of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and possibly also the farm unions, because this would give me something to consider and take to the proper authorities in order that we might resolve the problem.
I must repeat with regard to the turkey situation in Canada that there is tariff protection of 5 cents a pound, along with li cents a pound because of the discounted dollar and something in connection with freight rates, adding up to a total of about 7 cents a pound. In view of the fact this is about 20 per cent

more protection than most of our meat products receive it seems to me that in considering any change we must look at the situation very carefully.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: RUSSIA-REFUSAL TO SHARE COST OF PEACE KEEPING OPERATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Has Canada been made aware of the fact that the United States is taking the stand that the U.S.S.R. and other defaulting members of the United Nations must make good their assessments as a condition to the right to vote at the next general assembly of the United Nations? If so, does Canada intend to follow a similar course in this regard? Now that the stand of the United States has been made unequivocally plain, I think the house should be made aware of Canada's stand.

subtopic: RUSSIA-REFUSAL TO SHARE COST OF PEACE KEEPING OPERATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I need not remind the right hon. gentleman, of course, that the stand Canada takes in these matters is not necessarily the stand that is taken by any other country. The foreign policy of Canada has always been determined by the government of this country, and that is the way it will continue to be.
The position made known by the government of the United States through Mr. Stevenson was stated in a committee of which Canada is one of the 21 members. The interpretation that Canada places on the default of certain countries, including the Soviet union, with regard to peace keeping financial obligations, is that under article 19 of the charter of the United Nations, a country that is deficient in payment to an amount greater than its assessed contribution for the two previous years renders itself automatically liable to loss of vote.
This is the position as Canada understands it and as the Canadian representative stated it to be in the working group of 21. I hope, however, that this problem will be resolved without invoking the automatic application of this clause. I hope the Soviet union, and any other country that owes money to the United Nations, will find it possible to make payment and thus not render operative this particular provision of the charter.

Mr. Speaker, I think this question deals with the conviction of a man named Michael Sikyea, an Indian, for shooting a wild duck. subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REINSURANCE PROGRAM

speakeroldname: Hon. Harry W. Hays (Minister of Agriculture) moved
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REINSURANCE PROGRAM
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-129, to amend the Crop Insurance Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, before I go into a detailed explanation of the government's reasons for bringing in these amendments to the crop insurance program I would like to make a few general comments about the purposes of this program. I would like to point out, for example, that this is part of the government's whole economic policy, a policy intended to strengthen the whole economy of Canada by strengthening its individual segments.
While this particular program applies directly to our agricultural economy, we believe that because of the importance of agriculture to our whole economy this will have the broader effect of adding further stability to the economy of the country as a whole. In other words, this is a program that will benefit the people in our cities indirectly, while giving direct help to our farmers. We believe that with the protection afforded by this legislation the provinces will be able to expand their crop insurance programs as quickly as they feel it is warranted. We hope this will encourage every province to participate eventually, because of the obvious advantage, in a Canada-wide program. By spreading the risks in any one year over wide areas and a variety of crops, good crops in one section of the country will offset the effect on the federal reinsurance fund of poor crops in other areas.
As I have already indicated, while the main purpose is to provide protection for our farmers, wide crop insurance coverage will provide a new economic buffer against the effects of wide variations in farm income on the economy of the country as a whole. Crop failure in one section of Canada has its initial economic impact in the immediate area of the crop failure. But we all know that a chain reaction sets in as well, a chain reaction that eventually spreads through the whole economy by reducing purchasing power and often affecting employment in other industries. It should be obvious that anything that can be done to level out the great variations in farm income, variations which are due to natural causes beyond human control, will have a beneficial effect on all parts of our economy.

I should like to point out another aspect of this program which we believe is of as much importance to the taxpayers in our cities as to our farmers. In fact, since there are so many more taxpayers in our cities these days than there are in the country, maybe this aspect of the program is of even greater importance to our city people than to our farmers.
I am referring to the fact that this is not a subsidy program. Like the farm credit programs which this government has either expanded or initiated at this session, this program is designed to give our farmers the kind of essential help they need while at the same time costing our taxpayers virtually nothing in the long run. This government is not afraid to provide subsidies where they are needed, but we believe that wherever assistance required by our people can be provided on a self sustaining basis this is the approach that should be taken. We believe that the role of government should be as an instrument through which our people cooperate to help each other improve their living standards, and we believe the program envisaged by this legislation supports that kind of government role.
As early as 1959, even before the first crop insurance agreement was signed, there were clear indications that the provinces were not satisfied with the original federal role in this program. The minister of agriculture for Manitoba, Hon. George Hutton, indicated that without some provision for federal reinsurance of provincial risks he could not see how his province could make crop insurance available to a large percentage of insurable farmers. Other provinces also indicated that despite the provision in the existing legislation for emergency federal loans they could not risk the tremendous impact which a disaster year might have on their over-all fiscal positions. Their big worry was that large loans from the federal government to cover crop insurance indemnities to farmers in a disaster year would have a bad effect on their borrowing powers for all other government purposes. They also pointed out that in times of widespread crop failure provincial revenues for all purposes were sharply reduced, making it that much harder to contend with the demands of heavy crop insurance payments.
From the beginning the provinces operating crop insurance programs have been careful to limit the amount of insurance sold in any year, either by applying their programs to limited areas or by placing a ceiling on
Crop Insurance Act
the total liability to be accepted, so that in the event of heavy losses they would not be financially embarrassed. Crop insurance rates have been calculated on a basis considered actuarially sound, not only by provincial officials but by my department and the department of insurance.
I should also point out that these amendments will mean no change in premiums now paid by the farmers. The existing premium rate was set on a sound insurance basis; therefore the present premiums will provide provincial insurance funds with the capital necessary to pay reinsurance premiums to the federal government.
The provincial reinsurance premiums paid to the federal government will, over the long pull, equal what the federal government pays the provinces to help pay crop insurance indemnities in high loss years. Under the proposed amendments, provincial involvement in any year will be limited to about 25 per cent of the total amount of insurance in force in any year. As an example, suppose a province sells $10 million worth of insurance, and that premiums, including the federal contribution, are 10 per cent of the total liability, or $1 million. While federal reinsurance rates have not as yet been established, let us consider the rate in this case to be 2J per cent of the total liability, or $250,000. The province pays the federal government a $250,000 premium for reinsurance coverage, leaving $750,000 in the provincial fund for the payments of indemnities.
Now let us suppose the worst possible thing happens; a complete failure occurs on all insured farms and $10 million has to be paid to the farmers. The province would pay out the $175,000 left in the provincial insurance fund first and assume responsibility for the deductible 2J per cent of the total liability, or $250,000. This would leave $9 million in indemnities still to be paid, of which the federal government would pay 75 per cent, or $6,750,000, and the province 25 per cent, or $2,250,000. The total provincial involvement would be the 2J- per cent deductible of $250,000, plus $2,250,000 paid in indemnities or a total of $2,500,000 or 25 per cent of the face value of all policies of insurance.
This is the maximum possible involvement of the province, assuming that every insured farmer has a complete crop failure. However, even in the prairie provinces where, because of peculiar and extreme climatic conditions, a great variation of year to year yields is experienced, there has only been one year,

Crop Insurance Act
1937, when provincial average yields fell below 30 per cent of long term average yields. As insurance coverage is limited to 60 per cent of long term average yields, it can be reasonably assumed that indemnities will never exceed one half of the total liabilities, and provincial involvement never more than 12J per cent of such liabilities.
The legislation permits provinces to protect themselves even further, if they want to. The legislation provides that a province may, if it so desires, reinsure its remaining 25 per cent involvement with agencies other than the federal government, and that these additional reinsurance premiums, provided they are approved by the federal government, may be paid from provincial crop insurance funds; that is, from premiums paid to the province by the insured farmers.
As I said earlier, we intend this in the long run to be a self supporting program, but to be honest it is hard to say at this early stage just what it might cost the federal government in any given year. However, as I have indicated, the federal reinsurance premiums will be most carefully calculated on a sound insurance basis. The legislation provides that the reinsurance premiums may be adjusted upward or downward if experience indicates such action to be necessary, and the premiums will be designed to equal, over a period of years, the amount of payments made to any province under a reinsurance agreement.
All our expectations in this, of course, as in all other agricultural programs, depend very greatly on the weather. Obviously if we have a lot of crop failures early in the scheme federal payments will exceed federal income from premiums. But if enough provinces enter the scheme and the weather is kind during the first few years, income from premiums will exceed insurance payments.
For an example we can consider what could happen in Manitoba if the crop experience of the last 35 years were to be repeated in the next 35 years. If disaster years like those experienced in the 1930's came early in the program, a $25 million insurance program in Manitoba could cost the federal government $400,000 a year in carrying charges for the interest free advances which would have to be made to the crop reinsurance fund from consolidated federal revenues. On the other hand, if the good crop experience of the 1940's in Manitoba should be repeated before disaster years like those of the 1930's, then the federal government would gain more than $100,000 a year in interest on credit balances

in the reinsurance fund. And if the entire weather and crop experience of Manitoba over the past 35 years were to be reversed in the next 35 years, the federal government would have a revenue of $350,000 a year from these credit balances. I think this example should show how hard it is to estimate the probable cost of this program in its early stages, but let me repeat that over the long haul we expect it to be self supporting.
Aside from requests for reinsurance, there has been very little provincial criticism of the present act. The question of the level of coverage provided by the Crop Insurance Act is not before us today because these amendments have no reference to that aspect of the program. However, there have been some suggestions that the 60 per cent coverage provided by the act is not high enough for certain crops. In this connection I should explain that the policy governing the amount of coverage provided is that we want to guarantee production costs only, and no attempt is to be made to cover the profit portion of crop returns by crop insurance.
We are quite prepared to consider any concrete proposals from the provinces for higher coverage of certain crops, provided of course that such proposals are in line with this policy. I should point out that the federal government has no authority to initiate any crop insurance program in any province. The right to help our farmers in this way is the privilege of the provinces. But we are confident that with these amendments the federal reinsurance program will be in a position to fit into any crop insurance program any province cares to develop for its farmers.
If experience should prove this assumption wrong, or if a need to raise the level of coverage should develop in the future, I will be prepared to recommend to this house whatever further amendments are necessary.
During the resolution stage of this debate certain hon. members argued that these amendments are a threat to the P.F.A.A. They saw this threat in the provision that grain growers, whose lands are insured under this program, may be entitled to a rebate of their P.F.A.A. deductions. I reject these arguments as completely unfounded. In the first place, if they were true of these amendments then they would also be true of the original act passed in 1959 with the support of all members of this house.
The provision exempting farmers who insure their crops from the P.F.A.A. levy was included in the original Crop Insurance Act,

and the provisions in these amendments are only intended to give that exemption a more rational application. Section 9 of the Crop Insurance Act, passed in 1959, provides that the cultivated land of a farmer is not eligible for P.F.A.A. payments if the crops on any part of his land are insured. It also provides that the initial payment made when he delivers his grain to the elevator should be exempt from the 1 per cent P.F.A.A. levy. However, apparently because the previous government was unable to solve the administrative problems involved, the original legislation did not exempt any interim payments or the final payment from the Canadian wheat board from the P.F.A.A. levy. We believe we have now worked out those problems of administration, and that is why we now propose to extend the exemptions as we believe they should have been extended in the first place.
Farmers who insured their crops in Manitoba and Saskatchewan have been provided at the beginning of each crop year with cards issued by the crop insurance agencies. When presented to elevator agents, at the time of delivery of their grain, these cards exempted them from payment of the P.F.A.A. levy on the initial payment received at the elevator. These exemption cards were good only for the current crop year, and if a farmer dropped out of a crop insurance in any subsequent year he again became eligible for P.F.A.A. benefits and subject to the levy.
When the Crop Insurance Act was before the house in 1959 the then minister of agriculture, the hon. member for Calgary North, is reported at page 5231 of Hansard of June 29, 1959 as having said:
The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River also asked why the Prairie Farm Assistance Act should be ruled out. If a man has his crop insured under this scheme he will be getting a considerable return if he loses his crop and therefore he does not need P.F.A.A. payments. Hon. members must bear in mind that P.F.A.A payments are a form of drought relief. This has been extended to loss of crops from other causes but it is not an insurance scheme. It is essentially a relief scheme.
He went on:
If a farmer receives payment under the crop insurance scheme to which the dominion government has made a very considerable contribution there seems to be no good reason why he should also receive a form of relief under P.F.A.A. to which the federal government also makes a substantial contribution.
That is what the minister said in 1959 when piloting the act through the house, and certainly there was no indication then that he was trying to do away with P.F.A.A.
Crop Insurance Act
However, Mr. Speaker, the provinces of Manitoba and Saskatchewan have contended that we should exempt insured farmers from payment of the levy on interim and final payments as well as on the initial payments. They told us they found it difficult to sell insurance to some farmers because insured farmers still pay the levy on part of their returns from grain but could not benefit from P.F.A.A. in the event of crop loss. Under section 4 of this bill we are meeting the request of the provinces by providing that insured farmers will receive a rebate of any levy paid from time to time by way of deductions from interim and final payments.
In all fairness to the previous government, I think the minister had in mind exempting all the insured farmers' grain payments from the levy. In fact at one stage of the debate on the original bill he said:
At the same time, the farmer who comes in under the crop insurance scheme will not be required to pay the 1 per cent levy for Prairie Farm Assistance Act payments. In other words, he will neither pay into the prairie farm assistance fund nor will he be eligible to take money out.
However, I understand some difficulties were experienced because the P.F.A.A. levy on interim and final payments made by the wheat board is deducted from the net total amount of the pool before arriving at the price per bushel to be paid to farmers, and is not calculated individually for each farmer as is the case when the initial payment is made at the elevator. For this reason wheat board officials indicated it would be difficult to make adjustments for insured farmers when they were attempting to issue thousands of cheques with the least possible delay. As a result the original act when presented to the house only provided for exemption from the levy on initial payments.
We propose now to rebate to insured farmers at the end of each crop year the total amount of any levy which it is calculated was paid by each insured farmer on amounts received from time to time through the crop year from the wheat board. We propose that the wheat board, with the farmers' consent, will advise us at the end of each crop year of the total amount paid to each insured farmer. We will then calculate the amount of levy paid and refund this to the farmers concerned. The Prairie Farm Assistance Act at present only permits payment of awards to farmers to be made from the prairie farm emergency fund, This amendment will permit the rebates to insured farmers also to be made from the fund.

Crop Insurance Act
I want to make it quite clear, Mr. Speaker, that any province establishing an area in which crop insurance is to be sold does not mean that all farmers in the area are denied P.F.A.A. Only insured farmers will be out of P.F.A.A. The others will still continue to pay the levy and be eligible for P.F.A.A. benefits as they have been in the past.
I would further point out that crop insurance will in no way affect the method of determining the eligibility of an area for P.F.A.A. payments. Even in an area where some farmers are insured, if P.F.A.A. payments are to be made to other farmers in that area the crop yields of the insured farmers will continue to be included in the calculation on which the P.F.A.A. payments are made. Yields from all farms, those insured as well as those not insured, will determine the average yield for the area just as is done at present under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act.
We believe this program will give our farmers a choice they have every right to enjoy. The farmers themselves can decide under which program they want to operate, the P.F.A.A. or crop insurance.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REINSURANCE PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, having looked at the amendment to the Crop Insurance Act proposed by the minister I should like to say it meets the minimum requirement asked for by the province of Manitoba in particular, to afford some degree of protection against the possibility of substantial crop losses in any one given year. The success of the measure, of course, will depend largely on the type of agreement that will be entered into between the federal government and the provincial government in question. Since the actual amounts involved are not contained in the provisions of the bill, other than in broad outline, we will have to wait and see what type of agreement will be arrived at before we can determine the full effect of the proposed amendment.
However, this is not to say that we are not in favour of the amendment now before us. As I said at the resolution stage preceding the bill, I am looking forward to its implementation; because in my own province of Manitoba, where crop insurance has been in effect for several years, we have gained sufficient experience in the implementation of the crop insurance program to convince us that the program will and can be successful in insuring farmers against crop losses in any given year.

I am happy to see that Hon. George Hutton, who is largely responsible for the introduction of this measure in the province of Manitoba, is sitting in the gallery this afternoon, and I am sure he must be very happy that this bill is before the house. In the test areas that have been set up the province of Manitoba has been successful in covering about 35 per cent of the crops, and with the passage of this amendment the province will now be able to proceed further and within a period of two or three years should have the entire province covered, resulting in a total liability of something like $40 million. This is a considerable amount of money that is involved, and hon. members will appreciate the need for some assurance that in the event of a total crop loss the burden of responsibility will not fall entirely on the shoulders of the provincial government.
However, in saying that I feel quite certain we can take an attitude of optimism in predicting crop yields on the prairies in particular in the next number of years. As I said at the resolution stage, I feel that using P.F.A.A. records of crop yields in the past 35 years does not provide a useful guide. It is a very pessimistic approach to the crop yields that we can anticipate in the future because of the many advances that have been made in crop production techniques through the use of herbicides, pesticides, fertilizers and so on. It seems to me that in considering the application of this particular amendment we can take into consideration these factors which have affected crop yields.
I am glad to see that the minister is prepared to continue to look at the crop insurance program with a view to introducing further amendments if they are necessary in the light of experience gained. In the province of Manitoba a considerable amount of experience has been gained in the implementation of crop insurance. The Manitoba government has proceeded apace with the training of inspectors, field staff and administrative officers. I think one can appreciate the difficulty that is involved and the amount of time that is consumed in attempting to develop the type of organization that can effectively administer and carry out a crop insurance program. For example, I would mention the calculation of loss and the payment of indemnities. The suggested program did meet the requirements of the majority of the farmers within a province in the past.
During the debate on the resolution I was distressed to hear some of the comments made by members of the Social Credit party and

the New Democratic party intimating that the crop insurance program has not proven successful. I want to assure them that in the province of Manitoba the program has proven successful. When you take into consideration the administrative responsibilities, the task that is involved in training people to carry out a program, I think it is a credit to the province that they have been able to develop a program to the stage it is today.
There was some suggestion that the Prairie Farm Assistance Act should be amended so it could cover farmers on an individual basis. I hesitate to suggest that this could possibly have been done because, as the minister has pointed out, the Prairie Farm Assistance Act was based on the principle of relief. It is difficult if not impossible to change a program that has as its basis the concept of relief, into one that is an actuarially sound group insurance program such as this is. This legislation is available also-and I should like to point this out to the members of the Social Credit party who have been complaining about this particular piece of legislation being applicable only to the western provinces-to any province within Canada that is willing to take advantage of it. I see no reason in the world why the farmers in those province which are not now covered by crop insurance cannot make representations to their governments to have this measure made applicable to their provinces so they may receive the benefits therefrom.
There was some suggestion also that the Prairie Farm Assistance Act should not be discontinued. I am sure most farmers will realize that under this measure it is not being discontinued. As a matter of fact they have the best of two worlds. They are able to insure themselves under the crop insurance program and, at the same time, if they do not choose to become involved in the crop insurance scheme they are able to take advantage of what little assistance is available to them under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. It is interesting to note that in some of the better crop areas in Manitoba the amount of money paid into the Prairie Farm Assistance Act by some farmers would cover a crop insurance program, and the benefits to be derived thereunder would be much greater. Instead of the $800 that is available under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act there would be a greatly increased amount available under the crop insurance program.
As the minister indicated, the intention under this legislation is to provide for reinsurance so the provinces will not bear the
Crop Insurance Act
brunt of responsibility for this program in the event of a severe crop loss. This responsibility will be shared by the federal government. On this basis we support the legislation and look for its early passage.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, from the explanations which have been given to us by the minister respecting this reinsurance scheme it becomes all the more obvious that it is simply a measure to try to encourage provincial governments to expand their crop insurance schemes. During the course of the debate on the resolution stage many hon. members said that there seems to be a gap in the evolving of a crop insurance scheme that would be workable and acceptable to farmers all over Canada. As has been pointed out, only three provinces have experimented with crop insurance schemes, and this on a very limited scale.

I shall not repeat the debate we already had, because one or two further explanations which the minister gave this afternoon have set our minds at ease in some respects. He has said that this legislation, particularly that part of it which deals with the P.F.A.A. levy, will not in any way spur the withdrawal of P.F.A.A. from certain areas where it is now applicable. We understand, of course, that it does not provide for reimbursement of the levy to those farmers who are on insured land, particularly with respect to subsequent payments for grain. We realize the 1 per cent levy has already been exempted from their interim payments, and further than that I do not believe there is much more can be said at this time.
I hope all members of the house realize that until a workable program is evolved, based on the experiences the provinces have had, we will not reach the stage of having a comprehensive crop insurance scheme for farmers all over Canada. We shall need more experience from the expansion of the pilot projects already in effect. Even though only three provinces have made crop insurance available to some of their farmers on a limited scale, all the provinces have had the opportunity to set up pilot projects, with assistance from the federal government. I am not critical of the provinces for being timid or reluctant to go ahead with wide ranging schemes, because the risks, and the amount of money involved to meet those risks, would be beyond their resources in certain disaster years.
This bill will encourage the provinces to expand their schemes to some extent, and I hope with the experience gained in doing so it will not be too long before we have a comprehensive crop insurance scheme that will satisfy farmers all over the country.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I merely wish to make a few comments on Bill No. C-129, which has just been brought before us.
I see that the purpose of the bill is to authorize the establishment of a crop reinsurance plan whereby those provinces operating a crop insurance plan may, if they so desire, reinsure part of their risks.
I merely want to point out to the house that if that reinsurance applies mostly to those few provinces already taking part in the crop insurance scheme, then I do not think the bill is worth much, if anything, to the province of Quebec, for its minister of agriculture
Crop Insurance Act
himself did not see fit to take part in the previous crop reinsurance plan, probably because the conditions set by the central government did not suit him. As regards the purpose the central government had in mind, and the same thing applies to several joint programs, it did not consult the provinces sufficiently or did not even consult them at all, since I find that only three of them availed themselves of this crop insurance.
In my opinion, it would have been advisable for this government to present a crop reinsurance plan more consistent with the needs of the whole province-if it is so intent in establishing joint plans-since it was asked to do away with this particular plan among several others. If we had wanted to keep on taking part in joint plans, it would have been necessary to request a report from every province to know at least the opinion of every provincial department of agriculture, in order to have uniformity of implementation, and therefore all the provinces would have probably been interested in these programs.
Looking at the report on joint programs for 1962, I wonder why the province of Quebec has never been interested in the crop insurance program.
I have gone through the list of products insured under this bill and I see that many Quebec products, such as maple sugar and other specific products have been left out. That is probably the reason why Quebec does not seem interested. This scheme has probably been thought out by people from the west who may be fine administrators but who always think of their own interests first.
As I said a moment ago, if the provinces had been consulted, perhaps Quebec would have suggested amendments which would have made the former crop insurance program more interesting for the province.
It is often said that the province of Quebec does not get its fair share. Once again, it can be seen in this bill, because if we figure out the benefits, we come out to zero because it is the same report as in 1962.
I think that at this stage of the discussion of this bill, we should look for some formula which would be acceptable to the province of Quebec while protecting the situation of the other provinces and even improving it. But the needs of agriculture in Quebec should not be overlooked. Our farmers could get assistance when all kinds of disasters hit the province of Quebec. Once their sowing is done, the farmers confide in divine Providence, but they still have to put up with the

Crop Insurance Act
poor weather conditions without any protection from provincial or federal government bodies.
We are more or less interested in Bill C-129. In its present form it would certainly be of no interest to the department of agriculture of the province of Quebec because it is said in black and white that this bill is of particular benefit to the provinces where the old crop insurance plan is in force.
Honestly, I wonder why the government asks us to discuss such a bill when they know very well that only three provinces received any benefit from this crop insurance scheme. subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REINSURANCE PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the discussion on these amendments so far has really not been on them to any extent but on the merits or otherwise of the Crop Insurance Act to which these amendments apply. I think all of us interested in agriculture have been disappointed that greater advantage has not been taken of the Crop Insurance Act than has been the case. We have had complaints from two of the members who have spoken that there are only three provinces which have taken advantage of the act. It was understood at the time, and the minister has again pointed this out this afternoon, that any system of crop insurance must of necessity be run by the province because it comes within provincial jurisdiction. This federal Crop Insurance Act was put on the statute books for the specific purpose of encouraging the provinces, and providing help to any province that wished to do so, to set up a crop insurance act.

There had been for many years a demand on the part of farmers all over Canada for some type of crop insurance, and none of the provinces had been prepared to meet that need because of the possible large losses involved. Therefore we thought the only way it was possible to get a crop insurance scheme instituted in each of the provinces was to provide some form of federal assistance by which the federal government would provide part of the cost of such a scheme, and would provide the framework of a scheme into which the provinces could fit any individual scheme which would apply in their own province. This was done because it was realized-quite contrary to what the last speaker has just said.-that the agricultural conditions in the different provinces of Canada differed very widely indeed, and that a crop insurance scheme which would be satisfactory in Alberta, for example, would not be satisfactory in Quebec, and vice versa.
Therefore the scheme was drawn up very carefully so that it would be possible for each province to draw up a scheme of their own which would fit into the general provisions of the federal crop insurance scheme. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, statements along the line that have been made, that this crop insurance legislation is discriminatory, that it will only apply in certain provinces, that it will only apply to large farmers and not to small farmers, are not in accordance with the fact. The crop insurance scheme can be made to apply, if any particular province wants to do so, to any crop which is grown in that province, and the size of a man's farm is not the determining factor. It was hoped, as a matter of fact, when the scheme was introduced that a good many of the farmers in Quebec and Ontario growing specialty crops of various sorts-potatoes, apples, wheat, and so on-would come in under this scheme or that the provinces would set up schemes which would make it possible for them to participate.
I think there are two reasons in particular why the scheme has not been adopted more widely than it has. One is the fact that any new scheme takes a considerable amount of time to get into operation, for people to become accustomed to and willing to participate in. Particularly is this the case as far as agricultural plans of one kind and another are concerned. The second is that in all the provinces there was a considerable amount of fear that the provincial revenues might be very seriously and adversely affected if a widespread crop insurance scheme were

put into operation and a very disastrous crop year occurred in the first two, three, four or five years. The scheme was drawn up in a way which would make it actuarially sound over a long period of years, say 30 years, and I think everyone who has examined it is agreed that the scheme would carry itself. However, the provinces were naturally afraid that if they put it into operation and they had a bad year right off the bat they would incur large losses which would make their whole provincial financing difficult. The reinsurance provisions which are before us at the present time are designed to remove that fear in large measure, and I hope that the passage of this legislation will induce some of the provinces which have not gone into a crop insurance scheme so far to do so, and will encourage others who have to expand their operations considerably.
There is only one point I am wondering about in connection with the reinsurance provisions and that is the amount to which this legislation will increase the premiums which farmers will be required to pay. I have not yet heard anything which has made clear what that will be. There is no doubt that there will be some increased cost to the farmer in order to cover reinsurance on the part of the provincial government with the dominion government; I think the minister said there would be a premium of 2J per cent. However, I hope as I say that the increased cost involved will be very small, because undoubtedly just as with all insurance one of the reasons people hesitate to insure is frequently the cost involved. A large number of people in farming operations find this is true as far as hail insurance is concerned. Most of the farmers in areas subjected to hail have carried it for many years, but in areas not subjected fairly regularly to hail a large proportion of the farmers do not carry hail insurance, but take the gamble. The higher premium is of course a temptation to do that, and that is one of the ways these amendments might work against themselves if it means the cost will be increased to any appreciable extent.
As I say, Mr. Speaker, I am glad to see these reinsurance amendments provided and I trust they will produce the result it is hoped -a larger crop insurance coverage for farmers across Canada generally.

AMENDMENTS RESPECTING COMPENSATION ON INJURY OR DEATH
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the Merchant Seamen Compensation Act was first passed by parliament in 1946. Its purpose was to provide compensation to seamen who were not entitled to coverage under provincial workmen's compensation acts or under the federal Government Employees Compensation Act. This act has been amended on two occasions since that time, in 1952 and 1957. The purpose of these former amendments was to bring the level of benefits under the Merchant Seamen Compensation Act in line with the level of benefits available under the workmen's compensation acts, particularly in the

maritime provinces. At the present time it is found desirable also to amend the act for the purpose of bringing the present benefits in line with those contained in the benefit provisions of legislation in the maritime provinces. This is the first purpose of these amendments.
The second is to apply retroactively the present provisions of the act to widows of deceased seamen and their dependants and, in a number of cases, to orphans who were in receipt of benefits established under the amendments made prior to 1957. What we are seeking to do, as will be noted in the resolution, under this particular aspect is to provide for payment out of the consolidated revenue fund of additional compensation to widows and dependant children of seamen who died from injuries prior to June 1, 1957.
It might illustrate that particular aspect of this resolution to indicate that there are 16 widows at present in receipt of pensions of $45 to $50 a month, established under old awards, when at the same time the provisions of the present act provide for pensions of $75 a month. Merchant Seamen Compensation Act from age 18, if attending school. These two provisions are to bring our benefits in line with those prevailing in New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island.

speakeroldname: Hon. A. J. MacEachen (Minister of Labour) moved:
subtopic: ADOPTION OP INTERNATIONAL CONVENTION RESPECTING DISCRIMINATION
speechtext:
That it is expedient that the houses of parliament do approve of convention No. Ill concerning discrimination in respect of employment and occupation, which was adopted by the international labour conference on the 25th of June 1958, and that this house do approve the same.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am happy to be able to recommend to the house that it approve this important international labour convention. Following its approval by parliament we propose to proceed to ratify the convention immediately thereafter.

Labour Conditions
This convention was adopted by the international labour conference in 1958 and since then it has been ratified by 45 member countries. The convention seeks to promote efforts throughout the world to remove discrimination in employment and occupation based on grounds of race, colour, sex, religion, political opinion, national extraction or social origin, and to promote equality of opportunity. When a member country ratifies this convention it assumes an obligation to declare and pursue a national policy designed to promote, by methods appropriate to national conditions and practice, equality of opportunity and treatment in respect to employment and occupation with a view to eliminating any discrimination in respect thereof. In ratifying the convention a member country must also report to the I.L.O. regularly on the manner in which the policy is being observed.
The subject matter of this convention is partly within federal and partly within provincial jurisdiction. The obligation imposed by this convention, however, unlike some other I.L.O. conventions, rests essentially on the federal government. An I.L.O. committee of experts which has reviewed this convention states that it is possible for the federal authorities in federal states to give effect to this convention by, and I quote, "declaring a national policy and by pursuing it through methods appropriate to existing constitutional practice; for example, by taking direct legislative or other action in areas which are within the competence of the federal authorities, and by exercising their influence in other areas through educational measures, co-operation between employers and workers organizations, and other appropriate agencies as envisaged by the convention."
Clearly an anti-discrimination policy has been and is being pursued in Canada at the national level. It is implemented through a number of federal statutes. The Canada Fair Employment Practices Act has the expressed purpose of preventing discrimination in employment in the industries under federal jurisdiction, and the fair wages order in council sets forth a similar policy as regards work on federal government contracts. The Female Employees Equal Pay Act applicable to industries under federal jurisdiction prohibits differences in rates of pay based solely on the sex of the employee. The principle of non-discrimination in the placement operations of the national employment service is set out in the Unemployment Insurance Act. The federal-provincial agreements under both

the Technical and Vocational Training Assistance Act and the Vocational Rehabilitation of Disabled Persons Act contain clauses providing that assistance will be available without discrimination because of the racial origin or religious views of the person seeking such service. The Civil Service Act specifically expresses a non-discrimination policy in public employment in that the provisions authorizing the civil service commission to prescribe qualifications states that in so doing it shall not discriminate against any person by reason of race, national origin, colour or religion. The Department of Labour undertakes educational measures aimed against discrimination in employment with the advice and co-operation of employers, workers and other organizations.
So much for the position at the federal level. To ascertain the position within the provinces the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) wrote to each provincial premier to ask for confirmation that the province is pursuing by methods considered appropriate within the province a policy of promotion of equality of opportunity and treatment in respect to employment and occupation within the spirit of the convention. Hon. members will be pleased to learn that the response to the Prime Minister's communication to the provincial premiers was positive. We have received confirmation from all the provinces that they are pursuing policies to promote equality of opportunity and treatment in respect of employment and occupation.
Having received this assurance hon. members will, I am sure, agree that the time is now ripe for Canada to support this international effort to remove all forms of discrimination in the field of employment. Ratification of this convention has been recommended by a number of voluntary organizations interested in human rights. In particular the Canadian Labour Congress has made a substantial contribution toward the objectives of this convention and I want to express appreciation for this.
I am pleased to be able to remind the house, Mr. Speaker, that Canadian employer, worker and government representatives all played a significant part in framing the text of the discrimination convention at the 1958 I.L.O. conference. The text was developed by a conference committee, the chairman of which was Mr. Arthur H. Brown, then deputy minister of labour for Canada. The committee was tripartite, and the leader of the workers' group and vice chairman of the committee was Mr. Kalmen Kaplansky, director of international affairs for the Cana-

dian Labour Congress. Mr. Kaplansky was thus the principal spokesman for labour in the I.L.O. member countries on this subject. In the previous year, 1957, when the conference committee gave first discussion to the proposed convention, Mr. Kaplansky was also vice chairman of the committee for the workers' group, and the employers' vice chairman was Mr. Allan Campbell, vice president in charge of industrial relations of Canadian Westinghouse, the Canadian employer delegate at the 1957 conference. Thus Canadian representatives were spokesmen for the workers and employers of the world in framing the convention against discrimination in employment and occupation. Canadians having been so active in the drafting of this international instrument, I am glad the time has come for us to take the steps leading to its ratification.
At last year's I.L.O. conference, Mr. Speaker, I am informed that one of the reports described the progress being made within I.L.O. member countries, in accordance with the provisions of the convention, to eliminate the evil of discrimination in employment. The conference approached the subject in an atmosphere of some considerable tension, since the newly-independent African states had chosen this particular session as the occasion to demonstrate vigorously their disapproval of the racial policy practised by the South African government. The report contained a significant and sobering statement to the effect that no member country is entirely free of the evil of discrimination in employment.
The struggle against discrimination, then, must be a continuing one. The legislation which has been enacted in Canada must be seen as part of this continuing struggle, and not as evidence that the struggle has been finally won. As part of this continuing struggle the government of Canada, using every media at its disposal, has conducted a continually expanding program of educational publicity, to assist in removing the attitudes of mind that give rise to acts of discrimination.
Ratification of this convention does not constitute a declaration that we in Canada are entirely free of the evil of discrimination in employment, but it is an affirmation that the policy of Canada, at the federal level and and at the provincial level, is directed against discrimination in employment. Ratification of the convention will act as a spur to greater efforts to eliminate any discrimination which exists within Canada, and it will demonstrate 20220-569

our support of the international campaign to achieve this same objective in other parts of the world.
I	hope, and I am confident, Mr. Speaker, that this resolution will have the unanimous support of the house.

subtopic: ADOPTION OP INTERNATIONAL CONVENTION RESPECTING DISCRIMINATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased indeed that the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) and the government have been successful in obtaining the approval of the provinces to ratify this convention passed by the I.L.O. in June of 1958, and that they have voiced their opinions against discrimination in employment and occupation which may occur from time to time in the federal field of jurisdiction.
I too wish to join the Minister of Labour in commending the human rights committee of the Canadian Labour Congress who worked diligently, and its very effective members who, on many occasions, having had discriminations in this field brought to their attention, have referred them to the government. In Canada, as the Minister of Labour has pointed out, we have very few cases under federal jurisdiction where discrimination is practised in employment. During my term of office I experienced only two or three cases of this kind in approximately six years. However, in each case we certainly brought to the attention of the employers the fact that here in Canada we will not tolerate any discrimination in this area whatsoever.
It is to be noted that we have a peculiar situation in Canada in that we have provincial jurisdictions. Consequently we have to obtain provincial approval in respect of any of these conventions passed by the I.L.O. There may be criticisms that we have not approved as many of these conventions as we should have over the past years, but because of the peculiar circumstances here, because of provincial jurisdiction, and because many of these conventions which are put forward do not apply in practice in Canada, we have not approved as many as perhaps some people feel we should have.
A great many more countries which participate in the I.L.O. should adopt some of these conventions, which apply in practice to their countries; however, they have failed to do so. When one looks over the schedule of what has been done in the past he will note that some of these things which have been condemned by the I.L.O. are being practised in many countries. It is significant to me that many of the countries where the practice of discrimination, as condemned by the I.L.O. convention, is to be found, have failed to adopt

Labour Conditions
the principles recommended by the conventions. I am sure that all of us in Canada who do not wish to tolerate any discrimination in this area at all will be glad to support this resolution and give it our blessing.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: ADOPTION OP INTERNATIONAL CONVENTION RESPECTING DISCRIMINATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we too should like to join with the present Minister of Labour (Mr. (MacEachen), and the former minister of labour, in expressing our pleasure that the house is being given the opportunity to approve the ratification of the convention of the I.L.O. against discrimination in employment and occupation. I am sure we are all aware of how important in the world today is the issue of discrimination, and particularly discrimination on the ground of race. I am sure we are all aware that the chances of holding our world together might well depend on the capacity of mankind to eliminate all of the practices of discrimination that have been so black on the pages of human history. We were delighted that the I.L.O. conferences of 1957 and 1958 approved of the convention now before us, and we are pleased that a recommendation for its ratification is now being made to parliament.
In a way that is partly personal I should like to express my pleasure at the tribute paid by the present Minister of Labour and the former minister of labour to those of the Canadian Labour Congress who worked very hard for the adoption of this convention at the international labour organization conferences in 1957 and 1958. I am delighted that the Minister of Labour made special mention of the name of Mr. Kalmen Kaplansky, who was the leader of the workers' group that dealt with this matter in 1957 and again in 1958 and who, along with Mr. Arthur Brown and others, played a very active part in promoting this convention and piloting it through the various stages at the two conferences. We mention these two conferences of 1957 and 1958 because, as most hon. members are aware, an I.L.O. convention does not come into effect until it has been approved at two of the conferences of that international body.
Behind the efforts of the representatives of the Canadian Labour Congress at the I.L.O. conferences of 1957 and 1958 lie a number of years of very diligent work in this field. As the present and former ministers, and other hon. members of the house who have relations with labour will know, both the congresses which in 1956 united to form the Canadian Labour Congress, formed human rights committees a number of years ago. These committees worked very hard to get

legislation in the provinces and at the federal level which would outlaw discrimination. They also worked very hard to have steps taken which would lead to the passing of conventions and recommendations by the I.L.O.
Since names are being mentioned, I think it might be appropriate for me to remind hon. members that Mr. Claude Jodoin, who is now president of the Canadian Labour Congress, some years before he attained the high position in the labour movement he has now attained, was the first chairman of the human rights committee set up by the former trades and labour congress of Canada. Frank Hall is another individual whose name has been very closely linked to human rights efforts over the years. There are many others who were members of the former congresses and who have made very outstanding contributions since the Canadian Labour Congress was brought into being in 1956.
It was quite significant therefore that Mr. Kaplansky, who had played a very important part in these committees and in co-ordinating the work of the committees of the two former congresses, should have found himself in the position of being the chairman of the workers section of the tripartite committee at Geneva in 1957 and 1958. As a matter of fact, even since the convention was brought into being I believe a small committee has been appointed by the governing body of the I.L.O. to see to it that the practical results that could flow from this convention are achieved, and Mr. Kaplansky, who is the Canadian workers' member of the governing body of the I.L.O., is a member of the special committee that is working on this matter. So I hope the house does not mind my taking these few minutes to spell out in some greater detail what the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) and the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr) have both already done, namely to pay tribute to the part played by leading labour spokesmen in Canada to achieve this convention with which we are concerned at the present time.
I join with the Minister of Labour also in expressing pleasure that when this convention came up for approval at Geneva in 1957 and in 1958 it had the support of all three sections representing Canada at those conferences, namely workers, employers and government. It is a bit strange, of course, that it has taken quite this long, from 1958 to 1964, to reach the point where we are being given the chance to approve of this convention in parliament. I know that the same story has been given with respect to it that is so often

given, namely that it is because of our federal situation. Yet, Mr. Speaker, it is true that the International Labour Organization takes into account the fact that there are states with federal forms of government such as ours, and I submit that our record in Canada is one that could be improved.
If my information is correct I believe this will be the 21st of the I.L.O. conventions that Canada will have ratified and I believe that there are over 100 I.L.O. conventions which Canada has not yet ratified. We have been a member of the I.L.O. since it was established in 1919. We have paid tribute across the years to the significant role the I.L.O. has played in raising living standards around the world and in doing something to improve the dignity of those who work. We think that Canada could have done a lot better in all those years than ratifying only 21 conventions of that organization while leaving over 100 that have not yet been ratified. So we hope that the action we are taking today will not be so isolated, as indeed these occasions have been. Here we are 45 years since the I.L.O. was set up, and we are ratifying today only the 21st of the conventions passed by that extremely important international body.
May I conclude by repeating in a sentence or two what I said in my opening remarks. In this whole question of discrimination we are dealing with one of the most important problems facing our world today. If we are going to do something effective about this problem we must not only pass resolutions, pass conventions and put things on paper but we must have the legislation, we must have the means of enforcement and we must diligently set out to see to it that so far as Canada is concerned, and so far as any lead we can give to the world is concerned, there must not be discrimination in employment or in occupation or in any other area or aspect of human life. We are terribly aware of the problems in this field that are experienced in some other countries but we are not a people who can throw any stones. We still have quite a piece to go to make it quite clear that in no respect in this country, in terms of race, religion, sex or any other differences, is there discrimination. We welcome, Mr. Speaker, the opportunity that is being given to parliament to endorse ratification of this convention and we hope we will take other steps to demonstrate the significance of what we are doing today.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext: Is the minister saying this is the first time parliament has been asked to do this?

maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext:
With assurance of success that the request will be accepted, parliament is being asked to take steps in this important field. The enactment of this bill therefore will fill a conspicuous gap in the field of labour standards in Canada.
We all know, Mr. Speaker, that provinces in the past, in their jurisdictions, have established standards in the field of wages and hours which course has not been followed by the federal parliament. This measure establishes a record. It breaks new ground in that sense. I think in a second sense it breaks new ground also because it brings together within one bill at least four major areas of work standards, hours of work, minimum wages, annual vacations and holidays with pay. This bill brings all these together in a single enactment. I know of no enactment, certainly on this continent or elsewhere, that is so comprehensive in its coverage as this particular bill.
May I say that the short title of the bill is the Canada Labour (Standards) Code. The

conception of this bill, in its short title, will enable the house on future occasions in taking action in other fields of labour to use this main title. For example, if future modifications or amendments are desired to the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, the amended act might be entitled the Canada labour (relations) code. Likewise, if at some future time action is taken in the field of safety, the caption might be the Canada labour (safety in employment) code. It would be possible therefore to bring together in a single labour code all the enactments by the parliament of Canada affecting the rights and obligations of the Canadian labour force under federal jurisdiction.
The first reading of this bill, Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to report to the house, was received with approval both by the Canadian Labour Congress and the confederation of national trade unions. I had the privilege earlier in the year of addressing the national convention of the Canadian Labour Congress. At that time I told the members of the congress that it was the intention of the government at this session to introduce legislation in this field. This announcement, of course, was received warmly by members of the congress in convention. Later, I had a similar privilege of attending a convention in Quebec city of the confederation of national trade unions and the announcement made in the same vein was received at that convention in a similar spirit of enthusiasm. It is pleasant to know now that both congresses have approved the principle of this particular bill.
The objective, of course, of Bill No. C-126 now before the House of Commons for second reading is the establishment of minimum labour conditions for employees in undertakings within the legislative authority of parliament. The bill, incidentally, and more than incidentally, expressly implements the undertaking given by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) in the city of Hamilton on March 25, 1963, outlining the labour policy of the present government. As a matter of fact, a comparison between the labour policy of the Liberal party as set out by the Prime Minister, with the present bill and the important consequences following from this bill, will indicate that what we are hoping to do goes considerably beyond the policy announcement made by the Prime Minister in Hamilton in March of 1963. It fulfils also the promise I made in the house on my estimates, notably to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) to bring in a compre-

hensive labour standards bill at this session. Judging by the interest that has been shown both in and outside of the house, and by private members' bills which have been debated on numerous occasions on this same subject matter, I think the house will welcome the introduction of this bill.
If at this time, Mr. Speaker, I fail to point out the regularity with which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has espoused this cause and the numerous occasions on which he has introduced private bills, I am sure that omission will be pointed out by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre when he rises to speak on second reading of this particular bill. I know his interest has been shared by members of this house and his private bills, in this session and past sessions, have been debated vigorously and supported generously on the understanding that the government itself would be introducing a measure along these lines.
The fact that the intention of the government to proceed with this bill has been known for some time made it possible for me, as minister, and the officials of the Department of Labour to discuss the general effects of the legislation with some of those who will be affected by it and with representatives from labour and management groups. We have taken advantage of these meetings to discuss the general objectives of this legislation, and this consultation and discussion have enabled us to take account of some of the concerns expressed by making the provisions flexible enough to take care of unusual situations without affecting the essential standards or excuding any classes of employee.
There have also been discussions with the provinces. At a conference of labour ministers last March we discussed the proposed legislation in general terms. There was, I believe, general agreement on the need for progressive labour standards in Canada as a whole, and recognition of the gap that existed because of the lack of federal legislation. An examination of the statement issued at the end of this conference, bearing the approval of the provincial ministers, will justify that there was at this conference general agreement on the need for progressive labour standards, the acknowledgement of the existence of a gap in the federal field.
The problems of the setting of minimum standards are somewhat different in the provincial field jurisdiction, and we have to recognize it is the responsibility of each government to determine what standard it
Labour Conditions
can put into effect. Excellent co-operation has existed for many years between provincial and federal departments of labour in Canada, and we will avail ourselves of it for useful consultation on the implementation of both federal and provincial legislation in the labour standards field. It is a fundamental principle of the proposed legislation, not just as a matter of convenience, that the bill combines provisions dealing with four basic labour conditions as well as related matters. This has been done so that all employees within our jurisdiction will be ensured, as a matter of right, of as high a standard in these basic labour conditions as is within present reach.
The standards we proposed for the code are a minimum wage rate of $1.25 an hour, a standard eight hour day and 40-hour week, overtime hours paid at time and a half and limited to eight a week, seven general holidays with pay, and two weeks annual vacations with pay. As hon. members will have observed, the proposed labour code will cover employment on or in connection with any work, undertaking or business that is within the legislative authority of the parliament of Canada. The coverage is the same as in the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act. Hon. members will recall and realize that this includes mainly the transportation and communications industry, banking, uranium mining, grain elevators and certain work carried on by federal corporations.
The bill does not apply directly to employees of government departments or of departmental corporations. However, when parliament adopts this legislation covering national industries under federal jurisdiction, which I trust will be soon, the government will adopt as a matter of policy similar standards for its own employees, so that while the employees of government departments or employees of departmental corporations are not directly included within this act, the government will apply these standards to these employees.
In many cases of course working conditions of federal civil servants and prevailing rate employees are more favourable than the standards set forth in this bill, but where they fall short, my colleague the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Mcllraith) will indicate in due course the action that will be taken.
In the case of work on government contracts, changes will be proposed in the Fair Wages and Hours of Labour Act later in the session, in order that those covered by this legislation will also be brought into conformity with the hours of work and minimum wage

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion standards of the Canada labour code. So in effect, flowing from the enactment of this particular bill applicable to employees within federal jurisdiction, there will come consequential improvements applying these standards to government employees, and consequential amendments to the Fair Wages and Hours of Labour Act.
At present we have under consideration the amendments to the Fair Wages and Hours of Labour Act that will appropriately, and can appropriately, reflect the standards embodied in the Canada labour code. In my judgment it is a very significant step to apply these standards to the kind of contracts that are governed by the Fair Wages and Hours of Labour Act, and indeed to classes of contracts that are not presently covered by the Fair Wages and Hours of Labour Act, and I think in this respect that the proposals I am putting forward go beyond possible earlier expectations as to what might be contained in this proposed legislation.
In the first part of the bill standards relating to hours of work are established. The number of working hours is not to exceed eight hours a day and 40 hours a week, and where overtime of an additional eight hours a week is permitted, time and one half the regular rate is to be paid. Work in excess of 48 hours in a week is to be allowed only under permit, where the applicant has established the existence of special circumstances sufficient to justify working additional hours.
The officials of the department have accumulated considerable experience in the extending of permits in certain instances in the operation of the Fair Wages and Hours of Labour Act, and we believe that this can be a workable system under the Canada labour code.
