subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.

speechtext: The house resumed consideration of the motion of the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) for the second reading of Bill No. C-126, respecting hours of work, minimum wages, annual vacations and holidays with pay in federal works, undertakings and businesses.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the dinner recess I was referring to the provisions of the Canada Labour (Standards) Code with respect to hours of work. In the first part of the bill, standards relating to hours of work are established. Although the great majority of employees under federal jurisdiction are on a 40-hour or shorter work week, there are still a number of instances where longer or even excessive hours are worked in establishments that are subject to federal regulations. It is generally recognized that excessive hours worked over long periods of time do not contribute to industrial efficiency, are injurious to health and can be an important factor contributing to industrial accidents.
Technological advances and gains in productivity have already brought substantial benefits to most workers in the form of shorter hours as well as in other ways, and will no doubt produce more and more leisure time in the future. We must seek means of absorbing this leisure by providing for a more equitable sharing of it. The enactment of the 40-hour standard is thus intended not only to benefit those employees under federal jurisdiction who still work long hours, but also to help spread employment among the work force.

Without knowing the full extent to which overtime is worked in federal industries, the reasons for it, and its distribution throughout the year, we have not considered it practical at this time to propose limiting overtime hours more drastically but overtime work will be kept under scrutiny and we have made provision for reducing the number of overtime hours permitted by regulation. Such regulations could apply to the whole or part of any industry.
A recent I.L.O. instrument on hours of work, recommendation No. 116 concerning reduction of hours of work, adopted at the 1962 international labour conference, was tabled in this house by the former minister of labour, the hon. member for Ontario, (Mr. Starr), on January 22, 1963. At that time he stated that study was being given in the department to the instrument, with a view to action. The basic provision of this recommendation, the implementation, by gradual steps if necessary, of a 40-hour standard work week, retaining the 48-hour maximum limit set by an earlier convention which Canada had previously ratified, is essentially being implemented by this bill.
Mr. Speaker, I now turn to the second part of the bill, namely minimum wages. It has I think been accepted by all advocates of a minimum standard for wages in federal industries that the only practical approach is to fix a minimum hourly rate by statute, and that is what this bill provides. We propose an hourly rate of $1.25 applicable throughout the country. The minimum rate applies to men and women of the age of 17 and over. The charges or deductions that may be made for board, lodging, uniforms, tools or equipment may be prescribed by regulation. This provision is necessary to see that the effect of the minimum wage is not evaded.
A special provision is also included to cover the employment of young people under 17 years of age. In this case the appropriate wage rate for the occupation is to be determined by regulation. There are fewer and fewer jobs that can absorb young people with limited training and there is general agreement that it is now more desirable than at any time in the past that young people should remain in school to become as well prepared as possible for the more complex and technical world of work they will later be entering. Continuing studies are needed to determine what is and what is not suitable employment in these industries for those young people who for one reason or another do leave school at 15 or 16, and to fix an appropriate minimum
Labour Conditions
wage rate and other conditions of employment.
In order to ensure that the requirement to pay the $1.25 minimum rate does not stand in the way of bona fide training programs in industry, which should be encouraged, an employer who is providing a suitable training program for employees may be exempted from paying the minimum rate to them during the training period. I believe that members of this house will consider that the $1.25 hourly rate is a reasonable rate at the present time. We have to bear in mind that if, in an effort to raise workers' incomes, too high a minimum rate is fixed, it may defeat its purpose by making costs so high that employment opportunities for the workers it is intended to help may be curtailed as a consequence. I suggest that we should try to achieve a sound balance at our present stage of development, and to the best of our knowledge we have done so in the proposed rate.
Part III establishes two weeks as the minimum annual vacation with pay. It incorporates most of the provisions of the Annual Vacations Act passed in 1958, and repeals that act. The essential change is that the period of continuous employment necessary to qualify for the two-week vacation has been shortened to one year. This minimum standard will not impose an excessive burden upon federal industries at this time since the practice of giving two weeks for the first year of employment is now accepted in many cases. An important impact will probably be with respect to employees who do not complete a years' employment, who will now receive 4 per cent of their wages upon termination instead of 2 per cent. The provision requiring continuous employment for 30 days in order to qualify for vacation pay on termination of employment has been retained.
The fourth part of the bill sets out the general rule that an employee is entitled to a holiday with pay on at least seven general holidays in a year. He is to receive his regular pay for these days. If a general holiday falls on a day that is a non-working day for the employee-that is, a Saturday or Sunday when the establishment is closed-or on a week day that is a scheduled day off for him, he is to have another day off in lieu of the holiday. The principle of the bill in this part is to ensure seven days off with pay. It does not prohibit work on a holiday. Many of the employees to whom the act will apply are employed in continuous operations and normally have to work on some of the general holidays. Such an employee may be

Labour Conditions
granted an alternative day off with pay, which may be a day added to his annual vacation or granted at another time convenient to him and the employer. In other than continuous operations, where the establishment will normally be closed, if an employee is required to work on a holiday he is to be paid at a rate at least equal to one and one half times his regular rate of wages for the time worked on the holiday, in addition to his regular pay for the day.
The seven general holidays named in the bill are those which are most commonly observed as paid holidays in the federal industries. To take account of local custom in the observance of holidays, the bill provides that an alternative holiday may be substituted in any industrial establishment for any of the specified days. An employee is not entitled to holiday pay for a general holiday that occurs in his first 30 days of employment with an employer.
For most workers in Canada, particularly workers governed by collective agreement, paid public holidays are now a customary part of conditions of work. However, there is great variation in the number of holidays granted per year, the conditions surrounding the right to pay for the holiday, and the remuneration paid for work on a holiday. This code will standardize conditions regarding paid general holidays in the federal industries to the extent of guaranteeing seven days with pay. It leaves to collective bargaining the question of additional days as the circumstances may warrant.
The legislation will place a positive obligation upon the Minister of Labour to see that there is compliance with the provisions of the act and it will be necessary to have a system of inspection to see that the standards laid down by the act are observed. The furnishing of pay statements to employees is generally accepted good practice and will be required of employers under the act. A number of questions are anticipated in the administration of the legislation which will require consultation with the parties affected. Provision is therefore made for the setting up of ad hoc advisory committees to advise the minister on any matter relating to the administration of the act. There is also a provision permitting an inquiry to be made concerning employment in any industrial establishment, and a person appointed to undertake such an investigation will have the powers of a commissioner under the Inquiries Act.
Parts I to IV will come into effect January 1, 1965. This is to allow the Department of

Labour to make the necessary arrangements for administration and to allow the employers who will need to change some of their practices time to work out the changes in an orderly way. Special transitional provisions, it will be noted, are included at the end of the bill to allow a longer period of adjustment to the prescribed hours standard and the minimum wage, where it can be shown that compliance with these requirements would prejudice the interests of the employees or would be seriously detrimental to the operation of the undertaking. In each case a deferment may be permitted up to July 1, 1966. The opportunity for a deferment of the application of the minimum wage rate is limited to those businesses that are organized and operated in one local area. The purpose of this provision is to help lessen any hardship where the rates of employees would have to be adjusted.
Problems may arise in reducing hours of work in those operations which are now working substantially longer hours than 40 in a week at regular rates of pay. The principal problem that will be met here, of course, is a possible rapid reduction in weekly take home pay if the standard work week were applied immediately. For that reason this particular transitional provision is put into the bill. This particular deferment aspect is not confined to industries operating on a local basis but is applied to industries in general.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I should like to draw to the attention of members the relatively simple and straightforward nature of this bill. An effort has been made to avoid unnecessary complexity in administration and to minimize inconvenience. The provisions permitting the averaging of hours over a longer period than a week, permitting another general holiday to be substituted for one of those listed, and the recognition of the special circumstances of continuous operations in regard to holidays, and indeed the provision whereby the application of part I dealing with hours of work, or section 11, part II, dealing with minimum wages, may be deferred during a period of adjustment-all these make not only for flexibility and simplicity but are also designed to keep any disturbance to existing operations to a minimum, taking into account the major social objectives that are embodied in the Canada labour code.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in dealing with the second reading of Bill No. C-126 I want to say to the minister that I rather like this what I might call one

package deal legislation, which combines four aspects of jurisdiction in the federal labour field. When the minister said that these pieces of legislation which are embodied in the bill were breaking new ground I am sure that he did not mean they broke new ground entirely, because we have had on our statute books legislation dealing with hours of work and fair wages. This legislation provided that fair wages must be paid both on construction and on manufacturing contracts. Maximum hours on construction contracts were to be eight hours per day with a 44-hour week, and hours of work on manufacturing contracts were to be those current with comparable work in the area. Therefore, as far as hours of work are concerned it is not correct to say that this legislation is entirely new, but it does present a modification in that the bill provides a 40-hour week with the possibility of an additional eight hours upon application to the minister, and payable at the rate of time and a half. So in fact that is a modification of what we now have on the statute books.
We have had in this area many problems, particularly in the construction field, and I was wondering whether the minister should not have thought of making a division between some of the industries and making some things applicable to certain of the industries under federal jurisdiction with an entirely different set of rules for an industry not comparable to others vis-a-vis its work operations. For example, the construction industry is at all times uncertain as to the number of hours to be worked, depending on the season of the year, whereas other industries under federal jurisdiction are fairly stable in this regard. In this connection I wonder whether the minister considered applying a 35-hour week to certain industries which could operate under it. As we all know, in the United States there is now a trend toward collective bargaining so as to obtain a 35-hour week and thereby create more employment. This is a means that is supported by many people in their endeavour to reduce unemployment in this country.
In the area of annual vacations, legislation has been on the statute books since October 1, 1958. The proposal contained in this bill represents a modification. The legislation now provides for a one-week vacation after the first year of employment, or 2 per cent of gross wages, and two weeks after the second year, or 4 per cent of gross wages. This bill proposes that an employee will receive two weeks annual vacation with pay 20220-570
Labour Conditions
after the first year of employment, or 4 per cent of gross wages. I am wondering whether this proposal has been included to satisfy the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) who, I remember very well when I introduced this legislation for the first time, fought strongly for the proposition that two weeks be provided after the first year of employment.
The holidays with pay provision in this proposal provides for seven days. I should like to bring to the attention of the minister that the committee on rules and procedure in its recommendations presented last week suggested that members of parliament should be entitled to nine days, and that was done without any collective bargaining whatsoever. I think that was done for another purpose. However, this is a basis upon which collective bargaining can take place. The bill itself provides for seven statutory holidays.
We now come to the other provision in the bill which is entirely new to the federal field of jurisdiction, and I refer to minimum wages in Canada. This bill provides for $1.25 per hour as a minimum wage. Even now organized labour is asking for a minimum wage of $1.50 per hour. I am very happy to note that this minimum wage is to apply to the young people, 17 years and over. However, I am wondering whether it should not have been applicable to those young people entering the labour force at 16 years of age and over, because it is compulsory that children attend school until age 16, and many of them leave at that age to go to work. Consequently we have many young people entering the labour force who are not covered by this act. A great many of them must make overtures to the minister in order to obtain a fair wage.
The release for June of this year by the dominion bureau of statistics reporting on the labour force, indicates conclusively that young people, particularly those leaving school between the ages of 14 and 19 years, untrained and not having skills and trades required by industry, increased in number as compared with last year. Perhaps the minister would look at this situation to ascertain whether it would be practical to have these young people entering the labour force covered by this legislation when they reach the age of 16 years. It would also be interesting to know how many of them are employed within the federal field of jurisdiction and receive wages below $1.25 per hour. The minister did not indicate how many employees in this field

Labour Conditions
would be affected by this minimum wage proposal.
As a result of what I have heard I am sure that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mac-Eachen) received a great deal of opposition from his colleagues in the cabinet, but that his perseverance overrode the objections of those individuals who felt this was not good legislation. This is good legislation which I think will do a great deal for the economy of this country.
I was rather surprised that the minister in his opening statement on second reading said that federal employees would not be covered immediately by this legislation. I hope I am correct in that statement.

speechtext: They are not covered because they are covered by other acts such as the Civil Service Act, and prevailing rates regulation. Such changes would require special legislation. It would not be proper to make those changes by a bill such as the one now before us.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext:
There is no necessity for including those employees if they are now receiving a minimum of $1.25 per hour under the Civil Service Act.
I think this legislation is timely for several reasons, and I refer particularly to the minimum wage portion of the bill. I feel this will constitute a major addition to the existing pattern of progressive national labour standards, and I have in mind fair employment practices, equal pay for equal work, annual vacations, fair wages and hours of labour. The federal government in setting desirable goals or objectives in this regard can and does give leadership and guidance to the provinces, thereby tending toward higher and more uniform standards.
The area of federal jurisdiction in the field of minimum wages represents a gap in so far as regulation of minimum wages in this country is concerned. Though the provinces have minimum wage laws they vary widely in rates and coverages. I might point out that Canada is one of the few advanced industrial nations in this world which does not have national minimum wage legislation.
I do not know how accurate I will be, but I intend to list some minimum wage legislation that now exists in different provinces. If I misstate the facts in this regard I stand to be corrected. I understand in Newfoundland the minimum wage covering the general order for male employees is 50 cents an hour, and the general order for female employees is 35 cents an hour. In Nova Scotia the

general order for female employees is $21.60 per week in cities and towns with over 8,000 people, $19.20 per week in incorporated towns with a population of under 8,000 and $14.40 per week in the rest of the province. In New Brunswick the general order for female employees is 50 cents per hour. In Quebec the general order for male and female employees is 70 cents per hour in metropolitan Montreal, and 64 cents per hour in the rest of the province.
In Ontario just recently the minimum wage regulations were modified so that in some areas the minimum wage is $1 per hour while in other areas the minimum wage is $1.25 per hour. In Manitoba the general order for male and female employees is 66 cents per hour in urban areas and 61 cents per hour in rural areas. In Saskatchewan the general order for male and female employees is $32 a week based on a 40-hour week. In Alberta the general order for male and female employees in cities and towns with a population of over 5,000 is $34 per week, and in the rest of the province $30 per week.
In British Columbia the minimum rates are set on an industrial basis and there are 38 orders, most of which in fact set the same rate for both men and women. The manufacturing order sets a rate of 75 cents per hour for males and 60 cents per hour for females. In the mercantile, hotel and catering area the minimum rate is 65 cents per hour for both men and women. The rates in other orders range from $2 an hour, for qualified tradesmen in the construction industry, to 40 cents an hour for female employees in the fish processing industry.
We can readily see that this legislation will set a pattern or standard, and that provincial governments will be pressured in many ways to bring the present rates now on the statute books close to or equal to the federal standard that is being set in Bill C-126.
There is also a growing interest in the subject of minimum wages in Canada. Over the years that I have been in the house I have noticed that statements by members of the house have revealed support for a national minimum wage. This has also been urged by many groups, particularly labour groups, and over the years many members of the House of Commons have sponsored minimum wage proposals which have been discussed during private members' hours.
I feel that the greatest interest in this subject was created by what was done in the United States when a federal minimum wage was introduced in two stages. The first stage

was $1.15 an hour which came into effect on September 3, 1961, and this was followed by an increase to $1.25 an hour on September 3, 1963. This had very extensive publicity not only in the United States but in Canada and I think it did more than anything else to focus attention on the situation in Canada. I do not think there is anything to suggest that the widespread support of the federal minimum wage principle which was evident in the United States would not be forthcoming here in Canada also, especially on the part of the general working population.
Although some thousands of workers will receive wage increases directly or indirectly as a result of Bill No. C-126, which has as a consequence the establishing of a national minimum wage, I think there should be little adverse effect on the functioning of the economy generally or on most of the industries involved. I am sure that no serious employment dislocation will follow, nor would I anticipate that there would be price increases directly attributable to the minimum wage. On the contrary, I think that the resultant increase in purchasing power would stimulate production in other sectors of the country.
I might point out that it is noteworthy that almost all of the employment that will be affected in Canada is to be found in service and other domestic industries so that the effect of a minimum wage in those industries should not have any direct bearing upon Canada's international trade. I feel that this legislation is consistent with the present fair wages policy which applies to certain government contracts. In addition, as has been mentioned earlier with regard to another part of the bill, it will enable fuller implementation by Canada to I.L.O. convention No. 26 which has been ratified by Canada and which deals with the establishment of minimum wage setting machinery.
In some places in Canada the wage rates now being paid by the affected industries are below what are required by the law of the province in which they are located, and the continuation of this condition is becoming increasingly difficult to justify. This proposed minimum wage will admittedly add substantial amounts to the payroll costs of some industries, particularly banks, railways and telephone companies, but this should be kept in perspective. It would be interesting to know whether the minister has any figures on the cost that may be involved in those affected industries and services under federal jurisdiction.

Although this legislation covers a very small percentage of the labour force, I feel that its beneficial effects will be recognized by a markedly larger group and its ramifications in the future may be considerable if, as is to be expected, the provinces over a period of time bring their standards more into conformity with what this legislation will provide. The minister said in his remarks that the provinces were consulted and I remember when the ministers of labour were here in Ottawa. I am sure the minister made his intentions known to them, and if they agreed to this proposed legislation they certainly must have had in mind the consequences that would flow so far as they were concerned; and certainly they must have thought at the time they agreed to this legislation that in time they would have to bring their own legislation up to what the federal government is placing on the statute books.
From the human and more broadly social point of view the benefits of this legislation are very clear. Economically the country will gain in both the short and the long run. We welcome this legislation which comprises two new measures and the modification of two pieces of legislation now on the statute books, and I am sure it will be of benefit to the working force of our country. It will set standards up to which the provinces will try to bring their own legislation. I want to repeat again that I like this package deal respecting labour legislation which has been introduced in the house in Bill No. C-126.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have before us a bill to be known as the Canada labour standards code. It is a good piece of legislation and we heartily welcome its introduction. I know that on occasion it has happened that an opposition member has pleaded with the government to bring in certain legislation, and then when the government at long last brings it in the opposition member rises and says that the government did not do it the right way. I do not wish to start off in that vein. Rather I wish at the start to say that we are pleased that this important piece of legislation is at long last before parliament.
There are several things about the legislation that are particularly good to which I should like to refer briefly. In the first place I agree with the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) and with the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr) that it is good to have the various elements of a labour code wrapped up in one package. I was pleased to hear the Minister of Labour say when he made his

Labour Conditions
speech on second reading that it was possible that the other aspects of labour legislation might, after some amending of other bits of legislation has been effected, be put into a companion piece to be known as the Canada labour relations code. I think that if we could get all of the legislation respecting labour into one or two acts to be known as the Canada labour code, that would be a very good step for us to take.
My second observation in commendation of this legislation is that I am glad it deals with the four or five main elements which we have been asking the government to include in a federal labour code. We are talking about four or five elements, depending upon whether or not we regard hours per day and days per week as one element or two. I have asked for five things to be in a labour code and they have been: maximum number of hours per day, maximum number of days per week, a minimum wage, statutory holidays with pay and annual vacations with pay. The minister in his bill has combined the first two of those elements into one, so he talks about four elements when I talk about five. However, at least we are talking about all the major elements that had been either lacking or inadequately covered in legislation previously on the statute books.
When I say, Mr. Speaker, that we have waited a long time for this legislation, there was the fear that it might be a disappointment, that some elements would be left out. I am prepared to say, however, that most of the elements for which we had hoped are in it. There was one that was promised by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) when he spoke on February 20 of this year which is not in it. I will come to that in a few minutes.
The third word of commendation I should like to offer concerning this piece of legislation relates to the fact that it does fix certain minimum standards right in the legislation itself. As the member for Ontario (Mr. Starr) has pointed out, the tendency, particularly with regard to minimum wages, in provincial legislation is to leave the minimum wage rate to be determined by order in council or by regulation. The result of its being left that way is to have different rates in different parts of a province and various other anomalies. I congratulate the minister-I congratulate him all the more if he had the battle with his colleagues to which the hon. member for Ontario referred in getting these minimum standards-on getting the various minimums actually written into the legislation itself. This goes not only for the amount

determined as a minimum wage but it also goes for the determination of holidays with pay each year, to the number of statutory holidays allowed per year, the hours of work per week, and so on. I shall have something to say later about those standards in quantitative terms. But it is a forward step to have these things actually covered in the legislation as passed by parliament.
The fourth observation I want to make about this legislation, which I regard as good, is that it does seem to me to have the appearance-and I do not see anything wrong with the appearance-of giving a lead to the provinces in this field. Some of us have had the feeling, in recent months at any rate, that things have been going the other way in this country, that the federal government has been dragging its feet and allowing the provinces to determine things. Some of us have the feeling that there is a place for a strong voice at the centre, and even though this legislation will apply, legally and specifically, only to employees who come under federal labour jurisdiction, nevertheless it does give a lead to the provinces. The very fact that we have federal minimum labour standards will, I am sure, be good for labour right across Canada, including those workers who come under federal jurisdiction and those who come under provincial jurisdiction.
There are in fact, Mr. Speaker, other things that one might say about this legislation that are good, but I think I have established that I meant what I said a while ago when I indicated I do not want to be the kind of opposition member who is disappointed because the government has done what he has been asking it to do. Even so, I am sure the minister would not think I was really myself if I did not at least draw attention to the fact we have waited quite a while for this measure. I enjoyed the way in which the minister said this was an implementation, and even more so, of what the present Prime Minister promised in a speech he made in 1963. Well, 1963 is only last year. I cannot help thinking of the position the Liberal party took two years before the present minister was born; so some of us have been waiting a long while for this implementation by the Liberal party of its promise to bring in a national labour code, and of its promise in 1919 to implement in Canada the things that were called for by the international labour organization of which Canada became a member in that opening year of 1919.
Across the years many voices have been raised in parliament and throughout the

country for this kind of legislation. In another speech this afternoon I had occasion to pay tribute to those who had contributed in another field. I should like to pay tribute, as I have done on occasions in the past, even after all these years, to my distinguished predecessor and former member for Winnipeg North Centre, the late J. S. Woodsworth. He was a member of this house from 1921 to 1942. Mr. Woodsworth had many interests and he worked for the good of all the people of Canada. One of the things he fought hard for during the years he was here was the implementation of labour legislation, a national labour code. He came to this house shortly after the 1919 convention of the Liberal party. He was an idealist, a man who believed in people. He assumed that what the Liberals had promised in 1919 was some-think to ask for in 1922 and 1923. He did ask for it. It is the efforts of men like J. S. Woodsworth, the efforts of men in the trade unions and others across the years, that have finally resulted in our getting this piece of legislation that is before us. As the minister pointed out, both of the main labour centres in Canada, the Canadian Labour Congress and the confederation of national trade unions, have indicated their approval of this legislation, in principle at any rate. As we all know, it does represent, in principle, the kind of thing that labour has been seeking. As I have said, Mr. Speaker, we heartily welcome this legislation.
Now, let me comment briefly on the actual provisions to which the minister has made reference. I hope I might be pardoned if I make the kind of comment it would be expected I would make. First of all, provision has been made for a minimum wage of $1.25 per hour. I do not detract by one iota from my pleasure that the actual rate has been put in the legislation and that we are not left waiting for a decision by order in council so far as this matter is concerned. But the minister himself pointed out, as did the hon. member for Ontario, that the labour movement is now asking for a higher figure as a minimum wage rate. It is quite true that it was only at its convention this year that the Canadian Labour Congress changed its official position from $1.25 per hour to $1.50 per hour. But the fact is that the labour movement in this country has felt for some time that, conditions being what they are, $1.50 should be the minimum wage rate to be incorporated in this legislation. Therefore, though we welcome the fact that this is getting started, and while it is true that I am ready to commend the gov-
Labour Conditions
ernment for what it is doing, I am not going to stand up and say, "Let now thy servant depart in peace," because we have not really seen everything yet.
There are those of course who complain about minimum wage rates and argue that if they are too high they will work against the interests of the workers and the public generally, that prices will be increased, and that all sorts of dire consequences will result. All I can say is that this has always been the story. When legislation was first introduced into the parliament of the United Kingdom to try to put a stop to the practice of exploiting young boys as chimney-sweeps, it was said that that legislation would ruin the economy of England and would be to the detriment of the boys themselves. Perhaps it is a far cry from that to what we are doing now, but social legislation for the good of the workers has always had to meet this kind of argument. However, when we get social legislation that improves the conditions of the workers of the country, it improves the economy of the country and the well-being of all the people.
That part of the bill which deals with hours of work per day and the maximum number of hours per week, like the other provisions in the bill, is good, but there are one or two things to which I would like to direct the minister's attention. We are not satisfied with the amount that he has set as an overtime rate of pay, namely time and a half for the period of overtime worked, and we do not think he has yet grappled with the problem of excessive overtime work.
I did note in the minister's remarks that it is the intention of the department to study this matter as it goes along, but I suggest to him that if he is going to achieve real progress in shortening the work week for our workers-and this becomes more and more necessary as we move into more automation, more cybernetics, and more intelectron-ics, all of these things which will take work away from us completely-he will have to-take into account that as these things come about the 40-hour week is going to seem a long period of time in the kind of economy we now have. This aspect of the minister's bill will have to be reviewed. I shall have something else to say in relation to that, but I will come back to it later.
I now move on the question of annual vacations with pay. I welcome the fact that the minister has accepted the principle of one of my bills, a principle which the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr) could have

Labour Conditions
accepted away back in 1958, in that he has made the two weeks vacation with pay applicable alter one year. This is good. In my view it was wrong in the first place to make workers wait for two years before getting it. We are glad to see this improvement; but again this afternoon the minister reminded us that he was a guest of the Canadian Labour Congress at its conference in Montreal last April, and he was present when the congress presented its last brief. The minister knows the position of the trade union movement. Surely he knows it urges that, just as in other areas of life, other areas of endeavour, people in many instances do get a longer vacation than two weeks, we think this should apply also to industrial workers. The Canadian Labour Congress in April this year passed a resolution urging that at the end of three years employment the annual vacation should be three weeks, and there were other requests for even longer vacations following lengthier periods of employment. But perhaps this is enough for the minister to aim at now. I beleve that, having given us a bill that provides two weeks vacation at the end of one year, he should go one further step and provide three weeks vacation after three years employment.
The statutory number of holidays provided in this bill is seven, and the minister indicated that the holidays are named in the bill. I believe the bill calls them "general holidays" instead of statutory holidays, but the minister went on to indicate that it is possible to substitute other holidays for some of these seven. That is a good provision, taking into account regional and provincial practices, but I would like to suggest that the number of holdays stipulated should be nine rather than seven. I do not base that claim, as did the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr), on what we did in this house last week. After all, this house did not declare any days to be national holidays. We just made a decision that the house would not sit on certain days; but I would remind the minister that in the Civil Service Act there are nine statutory holidays provided for all civil servants. These are the seven that are in this bill, plus two others, Easter Monday and Remembrance day. I am sorry the minister has not included these two in his bill. I do not wish to make any distinction between them, but if I were making one I would say I am particularly sorry that Remembrance day is not included as a holiday in this bill.

So, Mr. Speaker, I think it will be quite clear that even to one who is pleased to see this bill, after waiting for it for a lifetime, there are some things in it which could be improved, and I hope we get some of these improvements while the bill is going through the house. We shall have the committee stage next, and there are quite a few clauses in the bill. That stage may take a little time, but I hope not too long. At least, Mr. Speaker, we will not lose any time on clause 1, and I hope as we get to the other clauses we can make improvements with respect to some of the matters I have mentioned.
I now invite the minister's attention to two or three things, apart from my references until now to specific enactments in the legislation, which I think he should look at. This afternoon he made reference to the question of safety, and said that maybe some day arrangements for the safety of workers could be included in the federal labour code. May I remind him that "some day" ought to be right now. As a matter of fact on February 20 of this year, as recorded at page 57 of Hansard, speaking in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) referred to this labour code as one of the most important measures the government was going to bring before parliament this session, and in the course of describing what it was going to do he said:
Now we will be proposing at this session a minimum wage, maximum working hours, standards for holidays and for occupational safety.
There were other references to that, both this year and last year, and I thought that was a pretty clear promise from the Prime Minister. Now we get this bill from the minister and all of the things that the Prime Minister promised on February 20 are there, except the one regarding occupational safety. I think the minister should get his helpers upstairs to work on this and incorporate it in this legislation, unless he can make the commitment that it will be introduced in some other piece of legislation this session. In line with the minister's own statement that he hoped to have this all in one package, I ask why not have it now?
If memory serves me correctly, in 1962-63 the last government prepared a piece of legislation affecting safety, so the people in the department must have this material; and if they have not got it I refer them again to the Canadian Labour Congress which can produce it for them. As I say, I hope safety

'provisions will be incorporated in this piece of legislation.
Another shortcoming in the bill is that it does not extend its provisions to the Yukon and Northwest Territories. I notice that my hon. friend from the Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) was over talking to the minister, and maybe he was talking about this. I know both he and the hon. member for Northwest Territories (Mr. Rheaume) are interested in this legislation, and I cannot see why these areas, which are so distinctly federal, should be excluded. If there were any possibility that they were to become provinces the week after next, or if there were any danger Premier Bennett was going to take them over and make them part of British Columbia, I suppose we would have to leave them aside for a while; but the likelihood is that they will continue to be territories coming under federal jurisdiction and, that being the case, I suggest that whatever labour standards we set up as a federal parliament should apply to the Yukon and Northwest Territories.
Another comment that I wish to make has to do with something to which the minister alluded, but I am afraid that is all he gave us, just an allusion-or maybe it was an illusion, if I may play on the word.

speechtext: It was not a delusion.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext:
The minister says it was not a delusion. We will have to wait and see. In his speech he did face up to the fact that a sudden application of a maximum number of hours per week could have the effect of causing many workers to suffer a reduction in take-home pay. If people who are now working 46, 48, 50, 52 or 54 hours a week- and there are such-can suddenly work only 40 hours a week at the same hourly rate they will, of course, have a considerable reduction in take-home pay.
The minister said this was one of the reasons for permitting some employers to delay the implementation of this maximum hours per week section of the bill. I understand that, but I think he has to go further than just allowing time for that kind of thing; I think he has to find a way whereby, with the reduction of the number of hours these people work-especially those who are anywhere down toward the $1.25 rate-there will not be any reduction in take-home pay. I am fully aware of the problems involved in this. I can see the minister suggesting that this should be the subject of collective bargaining, and so on. But we need not go over that
Labour Conditions
argument; we know the whole problem of how much has to be done by legislation and how much has to be done by collective bargaining. I suggest that when the minister is bringing in legislation for which the labour movement has been asking for half a century or more, he must see to it that the result is that it will not be seriously damaging to some people. This is one thing that some people who do come under federal labour jurisdiction are worried about.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, as something for the minister to think about pretty seriously I mention the word enforcement. He mentioned it in his speech; he said this has been taken into account and that there must be in the legislation and in any regulations passed under this act all that is necessary by way of inspection to make sure that the terms of this legislation are carried out. The minister expressed some pleasure in the relative simplicity of the bill, and we like to see legislation that is not too complex. But having in mind the amount of examination and inspection that has to go on in the provinces in connection with this kind of legislation, having in mind the problems that are involved in enforcement, I am not too sanguine that the enforcement provisions contained in this legislation are sufficient. I am prepared to give the minister time on this, but I think he must make up his mind that, having won the battle this far, having brought before parliament a piece of legislation that implements something his party promised two years before he was born, having won the battle in the cabinet, having got the provincial governments to agree that this is a good idea, he must go all the way and make sure that this legislation is going to be enforced.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, speaking on behalf of those of us who sit in this part of the house, and speaking if I may on behalf of the trade union movement, with which I am happy to be associated, I want to say that we do regard this as a good piece of legislation; we regard it as an important day in Canada's history that this legislation is being introduced-but there is room for improvement in it. The specific things I have suggested should be carefully examined before this legislation is finally dealt with and put through the house. I hope that serious attention will be paid to the improvements I have suggested when we are dealing with the bill in committee and I hope that as a result, when we get to third reading this good bill will be an even better piece of labour legislation.
