subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to say a few words in relation to Bill No. C-126, which is a bill that working people across the country have looked forward to for a long time, in that it will standardize Canada's labour code. It is not my intention to speak at length this evening, except to give my own statement of commendation to the minister, make a few remarks about the legislation and draw his attention to one or two points that go even beyond the scope of this piece of legislation. My own view is that this is a workmanlike, well drafted piece of legislation and that it will do a great deal to develop acceptable standards of employment across our country. No one can legitimately disagree with the objective of this legislation. Certainly it is desirable, it is essential, and we are grateful that it is before us.
Looking briefly at its different parts we find that it deals with four basic items of standardization. The first one relates to hours of work. I think this is commendable, and the way it endeavours to cover the entire field is likewise good, in that it sets out maximum hours of work as well. I note that in clause 7 of part I it specifically states that one day a week shall be reserved as a day of rest, and that in so far as possible that day shall be Sunday. This is good. Turning to part III, which is the section dealing with annual vacations with pay, this is likewise a very substantial and commendable part of the legislation.
In part IV the bill deals with general holidays. I would agree with the hon. member who has just spoken, that in view of the fact there are nine statutory holidays there can hardly be reason why only seven should be mentioned in this bill. I would hope that nine would be included, because I believe that certainly the workingman is entitled to those holidays as much as the rest of the public. In part V the bill deals with regulations and the administration of this measure, and in some detail goes into the specific aspects of this phase of the bill. This section of the bill is as necessary as any other part, because unless it is possible to enforce these regulations and make them effective, the bill will not really accomplish very much.
I do not intend to go into the details of this last section tonight, because we can do that a little later in the debate. I do wish to make a few remarks to the minister in relation to the second part of the bill that relates to a minimum hourly wage. I think that basically, to set a minimum hourly wage is essential. I think it is good that this legis-

lation comes to grips with this problem and states what that minimum wage should be. But it does raise a very serious question of policy that is involved in the matter of a basic, over-all, maximum wage which is set out in this legislation to be $1.25 an hour. Everyone knows that, particularly as a result of higher rentals and higher living costs in the urban areas, the cost of living to the worker is much higher in the urban areas than it is in some of the rural areas. This is true not only in rural centres but in provinces which are basically rural and do not have the industrial economy associated with the larger urban centres.
Basic wage rates, then, should be geared to accommodate this problem. In other words, with living costs higher in certain areas of the country than in other areas, we are endeavouring through a set minimum wage to establish a minimum living standard and are going to find ourselves in trouble in those areas where living costs are so much higher than they are in others. Therefore, if a person happens to be a resident in an area where the basic standard of living costs many more dollars than a worker living in another area actually what is happening is that we are doing nothing to set a minimum living standard, rather than just a minimum wage.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext: Do you think this will force every province to adopt that?

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext:
The hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Woolliams) refers to the different provinces and the problems which will result in those provinces through the establishment of such a wage. Again I think it has been clearly stated that it is hoped this legislation will set a standard and will be an incentive for all provinces, and not only provincial governments but municipal and local governments as well-not to mention industry-to bring their standards of pay up to something comparable and equivalent to this. Perhaps in this regard we will be working a hardship on these other governments, nevertheless I agree that in defining a standard you are setting an example for them, and certainly establishing a precedent which is nothing more than what is desired. However, I come back briefly to the fact that what is going to happen as a result of this situation I have just mentioned is that we are going further to drive our population to the urban centres, and I am not sure that this is going to meet the overall intention of this legislation. If a basic minimum wage is to be established it should also guarantee a minimum living standard.

Labour Conditions
I realize, Mr. Speaker, that there is a great deal of difficulty involved in how this can be done. Perhaps it would mean the zoning of the country into areas which would set a norm for cost of living. But certainly let us not be so optimistic as to think that just because we pass a piece of legislation here which sets a minimum wage at $1.25 an hour we have solved the problem of raising our living standard so that everyone can enjoy or be assured of that basic living standard. As I said before, $1.25 might be a very realistic basic wage in urban centres like Montreal and Toronto. It would be quite unrealistic in other areas-in the rural parts of Quebec for example, or in the maritimes. Perhaps in these areas $1 an hour would provide as satisfactory a basic minimum living standard as $1.50 would provide in urban centres such as the two largest cities in Canada. However, I understand that the government, and rightly so, wishes the code to set an example for all parts of the country, and to this end we can but give our agreement to it. But I suggest it will fail in this objective if the standards it sets are not practical ones, which is why I refer to this question of a basic living standard.
On another more general note, Mr. Speaker, I suggest a word of caution to the minister in relation to what we can hope to achieve, if such minimum wage standards are not practical, in the way of putting into the hands of workers enough dollars earned as a result of their own labours to maintain for themselves a reasonable living standard. I suggest there are three factors in our over-all economy which are required in the process of the production of wealth and fair reward. I am thinking specifically of land, capital and labour. One hundred and fifty years ago the economic situation of labour was such that it received only a very small share of the rewards from this process, and as a result the working man lived at a bare sustenance level. Gradually people began to realize that labour was in a monopoly position and that unless the owners of capital and land treated labour in a more equitable fashion they would be powerless to make any profit for themselves. So developed the trade union movement, which has done a great deal in the intervening years to raise standards of pay and improve working conditions for the working man.
Through the weapon of the strike, and through the power which labour holds in collective bargaining we find that labour has secured for itself a much more favourable
position than it had not so very many years ago. But, Mr. Speaker, I suggest that labour today faces a problem which is far more serious and of much greater magnitude than ever before, a problem which makes even the gains it has made during these years entirely inadequate for the problem it is going to face in the future and which it is actually facing in many respects today.
We are now coming to the time when investment in the shape of labour saving machines is reaching such a high developed form of monopoly bargaining that labour is being jeopardized. Through the development of the machine and the automation which comes along with it we find labour is rapidly being displaced, and with its displacement the money with which labour used to earn its living is no longer available to it. Supposing we were able to enforce a $1.25 basic wage rate across Canada; or for that matter, supposing it was raised to $2.50 per hour: In the long run what is going to happen is that the worker who is not worth that much on the open market is going to be dispensed with and replaced by a machine. That is the real problem which labour faces today. This is going to aggravate the problem of the unemployable, unskilled labourer. When we are talking of basic minimum wage standards of $1.25, we are really talking about that type of labour. Already as a result of that situation this problem to which I have referred is before us to a large extent. There is a real limit on how much good a compulsory raise in basic pay can achieve for any worker, and I believe we are approaching this limit at this time. Indeed we may already have passed it.
I suggest to the minister and his departmental officials, who I know are very concerned indeed about this problem, that the question of an adequate basic wage for the less skilled citizens of this country cannot simply be solved through legislation by means of a minimum wage standard of this type. Although we expect this legislation to pass the house and become law, and while we approve of the objectives it sets and the standards it lays out before us, on the other hand we must look beyond to the problem which is much greater than that. What must be ensured is that every citizen of this country in addition to his wages receives a fair share of the unearned income which is derived from the control of land, credit or capital as a result of the productive processes of the Canadian economy. What I am asking for is of course what we have been talking

Labour Conditions
about in our party for a long time, and that is simply a policy that will obtain a fair market return for every citizen's share in the wealth of our country, whether it be in respect of the natural resources of our country, or in the development of the means of processing these resources. I believe that our working people recognize this fact. I believe our friends in the New Democratic party recognize this.
The traditional means of improving the lot of the working man through the pressure of the trade union movement and minimum wage legislation, of the kind about which we are talking, are reaching the extent of their usefulness. We must therefore look in a new direction to accomplish the revolutionary new world cybernation, because even automation does not adequately today express the progress that is being made and with which we are living at the present time.
I suggest, as I have just briefly indicated, the economic direction in which hope actually lies for the working man, which will bring to him a share of those earnings and profits that are derived from the land and capital, and the direction that must be followed so that in addition to the wages that he receives he will be able to receive that income which is necessary to give him a respectable standard of living.
There is no reason why this problem cannot be solved, but many of our newspapers and economists in Canada seem always anxious to criticize any answer to this problem. They infer that this is a problem which we cannot solve, so we should be willing to let it pass by until we are in the position of being forced to do something about it. Certainly with the tremendous wealth we have in our country, and with our past record of ingenuity and enterprise, the standard of living we can make available for every citizen in Canada is something greater than we at the present time, or that this minimum wage legislation, will provide.
Mr. Speaker, I would just like to say to the minister that I hope he will give the leadership necessary to this house, as he carries out the responsibilities of the minister of labour, so that we may work toward something which is beyond this legislation, accepting the fact that this is good in so far as it goes, but recognizing the fact that we must do something far greater than this if we are going to give a guarantee of a basic living standard to every working man in this country.
[Mr. Thompson.}

Mr. Speaker, since the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) introduced this legislation members of the opposition have been heaping praises on him. Up to now the minister has not been criticized, but I think that in spite of the fact that he is highly regarded by all members he certainly deserves such praise. I hope that, in the present case, they will not be short-lived.
Mr. Speaker, Bill No. C-126 deals with several points designed to improve labour legislation in Canada and more especially with hours of work, minimum wage, annual vacations and holidays with pay in federal works, undertakings and businesses.
Personally, I feel that the legislation introduced by the Minister of Labour certainly augurs well for the future. That it is a good start. If legislation of this type is improved every year before long Canadian workers will enjoy better working conditions.
As to the 40-hour week for the workers, it seems to me that we have been hearing about it for years; as a matter of fact such talk must go back 35 or 40 years. In addition, over the past ten years already mention has even been made of the 36 or 32 hour week.
The minister proposes a minimum hourly wage of $1.25. A moment ago the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) referred to a $1.50 hourly wage.
It must be considered, however, that 40 working hours a week, at $1.25 per hour, only adds up to $50 per week.
But $50 a week, taking into consideration the present standard of living in Canada, certainly is not very much.
Besides, if the father of a family who worked for ten or 12 years becomes unemployed he will receive an unemployment insurance benefit amounting to about $36 a week. And if he can find a part-time job, he is entitled to earn another $18, which is half the amount of the benefit he receives.
This means that by working part-time he may earn $18 a week for 20 working hours; if he already receives a benefit of $36, he will then get $54 a week, and this to work how long? About 20 hours, at an average of $2.50 an hour, while under this legislation with the 40-hour work week, at $1.25 an hour, a worker earns less money than an unemployed person might make. Not that I think the income of the unemployed is too high. Far from it, for everyone agrees that they do not get enough.

A minimum wage of $1.25 an hour is at least something; previously, there wasn't even a minimum salary. It was suggested that the minimum hourly wage should be $1.50, which would amount to $60 a week for a 40-hour week. I am convinced that at the present time, considering the cost of living, taxes, and all that is offered for purchase to the public, everyone agrees that a minimum hourly wage of $1.50 should be our aim in the immediate future.
Mr. Speaker, there is a question I should like to ask the Minister of Labour. Having read, at the beginning, to whom this bill applies, I should like the minister, if he has an opportunity to reply, to tell us whether the bill will also apply to people employed in winter works projects in the various municipalities. Such projects concern the federal government, inasmuch as it pays 50 per cent and, in many cases, 60 per cent of the salaries involved. Moreover, those projects are not meant for the benefit of one or two provinces alone but of Canada as a whole, since they are carried out all across the country.
Will such minimum wages and minimum 40 hours also apply to workers employed under the winter works program? The fact is that in many municipalities we have seen workers in such projects earning but a dollar or $1.05 an hour and who often were not working 40 hours.
Another point which I wish to raise, Mr. Speaker, is that a number of regulations quite often come under such legislation. This legislation must be enacted, but it would also be advisable, while taking care that it is strictly enforced, to see that a new bureaucratic system is not laid on employers throughout the country. It seems to me that it would be possible to have this legislation fully enforced without increasing the administrative costs of employers, such as reports or forms to be completed, inspections, etc.
Consequently, the legislation should be enforced without increasing government red tape which already bears heavily on the employer. On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, there is another point which is not mentioned in this bill and which I would like to discuss this evening, because lately we have witnessed several glaring infringements upon labour union freedom.
The purpose of Bill C-126 is to help workers engaged in certain fields, especially those directly connected with federal industries or related federal industries.
Labour Conditions
In my opinion it would be most important to include in the act a provision under which the government would see to it that crown companies or industries doing business with the government do not act in collusion to curtail the freedom of labour unions.
Take, for instance, the Canadian National Railways. There is in that company an international union which interferes with labour union freedom of a large number of its members. Members of the C.N.R. employees union are under the yoke of the regulations of their own union. When certain members of the union want to leave to join another labour union-as in the case of Montreal stevedores who wanted to quit the international stevedores union to join, as a group, the national labour federation-then the international union, in view of the contract entered into with the crown company-a company, therefore, coming under the government- has the right to suspend its employees. It is not the employer but the union that is doing it. Although labour unions put up a long fight to preserve labour union freedom stating that the workers had the right to join the union of their choice, today the unions themselves are imposing on their own members the very thing against which they have fought. It is not common to every labour union, but only to some of them, especially those directly connected with federal government industries, that is labour unions to which Bill C-126 applies.
This interference by labour union leaders with labour union freedom or with the freedom of an important group of workers does not occur in other industries at the present time but only in labour unions of crown companies, such as the C.N.R. in the province of Quebec.
I have already pointed out to the house and to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines that the great majority of members of the international union of railway workers were anxious to leave that union in order to join the federation of national trade unions. But when the leaders of the international union realize that workers try to change their membership, even within the same union, then with the approval of the employers, that is, the crown company and the government, they have the right to suspend those union members who are no longer allowed to work for such and such crown company or government agency.
It is surprising that this only happens in government controlled companies or com-

Labour Conditions
panies which deal directly with crown companies or the government, such as the C.N.R.
In my opinion the incidents which occurred recently in Montreal and those which repeat themselves every year at the C.N.R. should incite the Minister of Labour to include in Bill No. C-126 a provision concerning the freedom of an employee to select the union of his choice, whether he works for the federal government or a crown corporation such as the C.N.R.
It has been suggested that Bill No. C-126 should apply to longshoremen and employees of steamship lines, railways, canals, telegraph or any other transportation companies.
In the province of Quebec longshoremen are faced with a problem at present. Nearly all of them would like to change their union affiliation, but they would risk losing their jobs if they did so. This is taking place within companies which transact business directly with the federal government.
I believe that questions respecting this matter were asked of the minister in this house. He must have received a submission or a request for the protection of labourers or employees working for the government or for crown corporations.
It would be appropriate to include in Bill No. C-126 a section whereby union protection for government employees and workers, would be guaranteed, while leaving everyone free to choose his own union or organization. This is the basic claim of workers and labour unions and organizations in Canada and throughout the world. Today, if unions or union leaders working for the government or for the crown corporations act in this manner, with the blessing of the government we may foresee the day, not far distant, when those leaders of international unions will do the same in private enterprise. Then we will see the renewal of the same labour struggles that have occurred in the past. Labour had won its freedom to unionize with great difficulty. I think that before all else within federal undertakings we ought to leave to these workers the things they fought for during so many years, namely: the right to join the union of their choice and to enjoy union freedom.
I am talking more especially about the dockers and the Canadian National Railways employees in the province of Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that it would be rather easy for the minister to include a new clause concerning this matter.
It is all very well to deal with hours of work, minimum wages and what have you,

but no mention is made of the protection of the worker employed by the government and of the freedom he ought to enjoy concerning labour union matters. This should be considered at the same time to eliminate what is happening now, and I refer to encroachments upon the rights of workers.
I should also like to refer to another point which might be of interest. We are dealing with nothing more than an embryo of a labour code in this Bill No. C-126 and, whether we like it or not, this is not a complete or comprehensive labour code as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre pointed out a while ago. It is but an embryo, the mere consolidation of certain points of the labour code, when what we should have is more complete labour legislation.
Another point could be included also in this embryo of a labour code. It would be the protection of crown corporations or government employees against decisions taken by some high officials.
It seems to me that the government worker, or the one employed by a crown corporation or an organization that deals with the government, who is not satisfied with a decision taken by certain high officials, should have the right of appeal to some organization, independent from the crown corporation or the department that employs him.
In this connection I would like to give an example. There are several such cases, at least within crown corporations or departments mentioned in Bill No. C-126.
I would like to quote the case of an individual who worked for the C.N.R. for a long time, some 30 years. Eleven years before his retirement he was appointed foreman, but three months before drawing his pension he was demoted and his pension reduced accordingly. Then, as he was not satisfied, he could only appeal to the officials of his company. That is precisely what happened in the case of a C.N.R. employee, a man from Jonquiere who held a position of foreman or something like that for 11 years; three months before he reached the age of 65 at which time he was to retire, he was demoted to a less important position. Naturally his pension was reduced accordingly even though he had held a higher position for 11 years.
Such an employee can only appeal to his superiors, the very people who ruled against him in the first place. He cannot appeal to some independent body outside the crown corporation for which he works. In a case like

that, the officials who took the original decision are not very likely to reconsider their ruling. The higher echelon of the administration is not interested in matters pertaining to lower employees and they let intermediate officials rule on the case. Consequently, the hapless C.N.R. employee can only appeal to those who have already decided against him. His rights are infringed upon and he does not even have the consolation of saying that his case has been judged by an independent or impartial body.
Under the circumstances, would the minister consider the possibility of including in his draft labour code a provision setting up a body which would be independent of all government departments and crown corporations and to which an employee could appeal if he is not satisfied with a decision taken by his employer? In addition, he could appeal to that organization without incurring substantial or excessive costs which, in many cases, prevent him from lodging such an appeal.
Therefore, it seems to me that a provision designed to set up an independent organization could be added to Bill No. C-126, so as to improve it while providing a further guarantee to federal civil servants and crown corporation employees. This would not entail any exceptional expenditures, but would contribute to provide workers and employees coming under Bill No. C-126 with an additional guarantee in this draft labour code.
There is another point I should like to deal with for a few minutes. Those mainly concerned are people employed by the federal government, crown corporations and agencies dealing with the federal government. This means that in those fields, at least in the majority of those fields-because there are some who are not in the three classes I have mentioned-the great majority of the employees affected by this bill are labourers or employees working directly or indirectly for the government since they work for a crown corporation. Then it is the federal government itself which has direct or indirect authority over those employees. This is what one may call the civil service. The state or the government might give some protection to this official; the protection to use the language of his own choice.
We often see this abnormal situation in some places like my riding of Lapointe, Jonquiere, for instance, where there is a C.N.R. warehouse or a maintenance plant-now it does not happen so often as before, one must admit that there is an improvement, at least in Jonquiere, and the labourers of Jonquiere
Labour Conditions
and the C.N.R. employees in that centre told me that there was much inprovement -but in other cities of the province of Quebec, and even also in several other places, there is not enough respect for the language of the labourer, so that if he wants to write to a high official to make certain recommendations or apply for a job which is vacant an employee of a higher grade left or retired, he has to do it on an English form and must write in English to his superior. Inevitably, this employee, working in an almost exclusively French Canadian environment, quite often in a repair factory, did not have the opportunity or the advantage of learning to speak English to the extent he would have wished. Therefore, it is all the more difficult for him to apply for a superior position where the knowledge of a language other than his own is necessary. For him, this is a considerable handicap.
My third suggestion to the minister-and it would not be difficult to include it in the bill-is that a clause should be added to this labour code to the effect that any government employee or any employee of a crown corporation could use the language he knows best in his relations with his superiors. I would like the minister to listen to this suggestion, because in my opinion he would find it important.
It seems, Mr. Speaker, that all too often when one makes suggestions to the minister during the discussion on the motion for second reading, other members sit beside him and attempt to speak to him or engage in a conversation with him. I do not know whether it is to claim benefits for their own constituencies, but, in any event, they are perhaps disturbing the minister, and it would do him a service to ask others to cease representations to the minister for political favours, so that he may listen to the suggestions we have to make to him.
The minister admitted a moment ago that it was difficult to combine the 40-hour week with the $1.25 minimum wage; maybe so, but in my opinion it would be timely to add a clause at the beginning of the labour code, in which it would be mentioned that an employee of a crown corporation or of the federal government, in his relations with his supervisors, would be entitled to speak to him in the language that is best known to him.
It seems to me that it would then be rendering them justice; it would be substituting or replacing something which exists at

Labour Conditions
the present time and which is outdated, and should not exist, by something concrete.
All officials require that employees write to them in English rather than in the language with which the employee is more familiar. To let civil servants or crown corporation employees use one or the other of the official languages would be a protection and a guarantee of their rights and privileges, that is to be able to express themselves in the language which they know best.
I commend the minister for introducing this bill today. I am sending him a dozen roses and a bouquet of flowers, and I will send him another dozen roses and another bouquet of flowers if he wants to take into consideration the remarks we have just made in this connection, that is to try and protect the freedom of labour unions in crown corporations and in the various government departments and to set up an agency entirely free from crown corporations, or any department, to which a federal civil servant could appeal if he is not satisfied with a decision taken by a crown corporation or a department official. Employees will then be assured of impartiality and be protected against any linguistic discrimination which may exist.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, Bill No. C-126 will require improvements and the same as Rome, which was not built in one day, the labour code will not be perfect in the space of one week.
If the Minister of Labour shows as much good will as he displayed in introducing Bill No. C-126, there is every reason to believe and to hope that before long Canada will have better labour legislation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too would like to compliment the Minister of Labour and the government for introducing this legislation. I, like many of my colleagues on this side of the house, regard it as one of the principal features of the labour program that was drafted and put forward to the Canadian people by the Liberal party prior to the 1962-63 campaigns. So, to that degree when I see a government proposal coming before the house, a proposal on all fours with the principal features of its labour platform in two elections, it cannot help but afford considerable satisfaction.
I could not help but note that when the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) was speaking he referred to a time as far back as 1919 when dealing with various aspects of this measure. I hope the hon. member will forgive me when I ask him to realize
[Mr. Gregoire.l
that I am not so preoccupied with the past, but am more vitally concerned to see the proposals we advanced prior to the last two election campaigns being implemented in legislation. I am thoroughly satisfied that this is being done. In fact I was almost overcome by that hon. member's complimentary remarks, in many spots throughout his speech, in reference to this government. I noticed how mellow he was with respect to certain features of the bill; I am unaccustomed to hear him speak in this fashion. In fact I hope next time he comes down to Hamilton East he will talk in the same vein there.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. member would read the whole of my speech in Hamilton East.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
As has been stated, this bill packages into one, five main elements that have been talked about for a long time. It provides for a minimum wage of $1.25 an hour, for a 40 hour week, for a limit of eight hours per day, for annual vacations of two weeks with pay and for seven statutory holidays. The annual vacation of two weeks is to be after one year's employment, and it also provides for overtime of eight hours on a 40-hour week. In fact it includes much of the suggested legislation put forward by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and others, and certainly embodies completely the points that were proposed by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) when he spoke in Hamilton just prior to the 1963 election.
One of the fine things we can hope for from this legislation is that it will cause pressure to be exerted on provincial legislatures to adopt similar legislation which will in effect cover the whole labour force. One of the things which contributed to the interest taken by so many members of all parties in minimum wage legislation and other minimum standards was the well known scandal in the Toronto area, which occurred in the construction trades. After the investigation which was held with respect to it, everyone was convinced that many thousands of employees were being exploited to a most considerable degree. One of the principal recommendations of the inquiring commission was that a minimum labour standard of minimum wage be adopted by the provincial government, and if this present legislation contributes to introducing this type of measure across the board we shall see the end of that kind of exploitation.

In my own city of Hamilton it is not uncommon to find construction workers, in many cases working for non-union contractors, making far less than $1.25 an hour. This legislation will help all such areas where wages are less than $1.25 an hour. We sometimes forget there are many people in urban areas who do not get $1.25 an hour, and I hope this legislation will provide a stimulus to provincial legislatures to adopt similar measures.
Filibuster.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
It is interesting to hear the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) call "filibuster". I have never heard an hon. member take up more time of the house on trivialities than he. One thing which has not been emphasized is the fact that this legislation provides minimum standards. Nobody on this side of the house pretends these standards should be the set standards, and that people should not get better standards. These are minimum standards and should be regarded as such.
Recently the United States has talked much about the question of poverty, and it seems to me that the discussion of poverty is just getting under way in Canada. One principal speech was made on it by the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) some months ago.
You have talked it out.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the remarks I intend to make tonight on the late show are in relation to a question which I asked the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources with reference to our national parks, as recorded at page 8872 of Hansard for Thursday last, as follows:
I would like to direct a question to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources concerning Banff. I will put my question in two parts. Is the minister prepared now to meet the elected council of Banff; and second, is he not well aware that one of our land developers of Alberta, namely Mayor Hawrelak, is the man behind the syndicate building this particular motel in that area which is zoned against this kind of development?
I have only seven minutes to deal with this question and that makes it difficult, but first I would like to refer to page 8021 of Hansard for Tuesday, September 15, where the minister was recorded as answering a question by the former minister of northern affairs, in reference to this very matter. He said this:
Mr. Speaker, I will first of all disappoint the hon. member by telling him that I have no intention of resigning.
The Banff council, which is a democratic organization, elected by the people of Banff, have asked for the resignation of the minister on the grounds, first of all that he will not answer their letters, and second that he will not listen to any of the decisions they make. I would like to hear from the minister in that regard. He may have another side of the picture now, but this is exactly what his answer was:
This is an advisory body. In the past we have thought that in these unorganized areas within our parks such bodies were good things.
Then he said:
After the decision taken last evening-
Of course, that was asking for his resignation:
-I am going to be more cautious about the advice-
And I do not blame him:
-I accept from that particular body.
Two of the reasons given for the action were that we were running contrary to the Oberlander report, and were running contrary to recommends-
9018	HOUSE OF
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion tions of the land use code. On checking into the matter I find that in the allocation of this particular property for a motel we are following the Oberlander report completely, and in addition we are following the advice of the body involved in respect of the zoning plans. So I cannot understand how they can be so ill-informed, that I shall be very careful about taking any advice from them in the future.
As I understand the minister's position, he has now agreed to meet this democratic organization; but he does not want to meet those people who made that suggestion-he will only meet part of the body. This is a ridiculous position to be in. I say to the minister that if he is going to meet this elected body, whether he likes them or not he should meet with them because they are an elected body in Banff. What is the problem? I mentioned the point about our great land developer and the syndicate. I refer to Mayor Hawrelak, mayor of Edmonton. There is no doubt about it, that because of relatives of his who are behind this particular man, he is behind the promotion in question.
What are they doing? They are agreeing, contrary to the recommendations of the interim development board and contrary to the advisory council, to build a motel in one of the best residential sections of Banff. I say this is contrary to the spirit of the National Parks Act, which is really to preserve the parks in their natural and national beauty. I put this to the minister first of all; I ask him to check tonight-and I am most serious about this-order in council No. 1,149 of 1956. I see the minister making a note of this. He will find this order in council most interesting. It zoned this area for residential purposes, or as a dual residential area, and is against the building of a motel or hotel in this area. This is one of the most beautiful spots in Banff national park; second, it is in the best residential area of those people who are serving the tourists. I say that the development in question is against the law and I would ask the minister to check into this question very carefully.

maintopic: NATIONAL PARKS-BANFF-MEETING WITH COUNCIL RESPECTING MOTEL CONSTRUCTION
speechtext: Wasn't Hawrelak going to be a cabinet minister?

maintopic: NATIONAL PARKS-BANFF-MEETING WITH COUNCIL RESPECTING MOTEL CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
He was, but Mr. Justice Porter, who has great vision and is one of the better members of the judiciary, unseated him in another capacity. But I do not want to be sidetracked. The minister, in approving this development, is in breach of the spirit of the National Parks Act and the Oberlander report. I ask the minister to look at pages 48 to 52 of the Oberlander report. He says that in fact this is not against the


Oberlander report. First of all I would point out that it is against an order in council, and if there is a zoning bylaw contained in an order in council passed by the former Liberal government, I do not know how the minister can usurp that law.
I say that although there is a chart showing this area as a parking area and possibly a motel area, it is because there is a motel behind the area and it is not really zoned for motels. Page 48 of the Oberlander report recommends that this area be kept in its present state, in its beautiful residential state, but particularly in its beautiful state. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I say there is something behind this plan. I would not make this charge against the minister because I am not that kind of fellow, but the advisory council did suggest there is something bad in this connection, that something smells in the state of Denmark, or there is some patronage. I am not saying this to the minister, but I am saying that there is so much area in the townsite of Banff and so much area in the whole of the national park, which is as big as the province of Prince Edward Island, that they could build this motel in a place other than that approved by the minister, which is contrary to the recommendations of the interim development board. On the board are two of the top officials, Mr. Strong and Mr. Dempster. When you have had a submission from a democratic organization and from the people of Banff which is contrary to the law then there is something wrong.
I am not going to discuss tonight the elected body in Banff. They are a body which demanded your resignation, sir, because they said this was patronage and that there was a pay-off. I do not know about that but I do say, let us be reasonable. They are tearing down an old building in that particular spot now. Let us leave it in its natural state. There are lots of other areas in the townsite of Banff. Why can there not be a trade or a compromise where even this great land developer of ours can build? The last time he made half a million dollars out of a similar project.

maintopic: NATIONAL PARKS-BANFF-MEETING WITH COUNCIL RESPECTING MOTEL CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the question addressed to me by the hon. member is divided into two parts. The first is: Am I now prepared to meet the advisory committee? Under date October 9 I wrote them and I do not think I could do

better than read at this time a portion of this letter:
In my opinion the improvement to the Bow View Lodge site was entirely necessary to add to the range of accommodation available in the Banff townsite.
Until this episode I have valued the advice of the Banff advisory council and my good relationship with its members. In national park development the advice of those whose income is derived from the parks is naturally to be valued. It is also necessary to take the advice of those who seek the enjoyment of the national parks as visitors and as part of the Canadian public. The balancing of these interests is never an easy task and it is made more difficult where conclusion drawing appears to be based on suspicion and supposition.
It is a matter of the deepest regret to me that statements have been attributed to certain members of the council charging me or my officials with decisions motivated for reasons of patronage, or I believe the word used was "pay off". Such statements are absolutely untrue and beneath contempt. If the members of council have any doubt then I invite them to take the necessary legal proceedings to have the matter determined. In the alternative I request council to repudiate such allegations and any members of council responsible for them.
I have always been willing to speak to or meet with the Banff advisory council or any of the members when meetings could reasonably be arranged. On Monday, October 5, you were approached by an official of my department in Banff with the advice that I would be prepared to meet the Banff advisory council during the afternoon of Saturday, October 24, in Calgary, at which day I would be visiting that city. I am advised that in reply you stated that the council would not be in a position to decide until October 19 whether it would meet with me. If this attitude of yourself is not correctly reported, then I would be obliged to have your statement.
I am still prepared to see the members of the Banff advisory council in Calgary on the afternoon of October 24 but so far as I am concerned it will be the last meeting which I hold with the present or any future Banff advisory council until I have received their decision on my request from council concerning its collective responsibility for the statements alleging political patronage and "pay off" which I have mentioned.
I trust that my position is now clear and I look forward to having your response in due course.

TRANSPORTATION-QUEBEC-PROPOSED REDUCTION IN C.P.R. TRAIN SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I apologize for keeping you late tonight, but I believe that this matter is worthwhile.
On Friday last I asked the following question:
Mr. Speaker, I had a question for the Minister of Transport but, in his absence, I shall put it to the acting minister.
Could the minister ask the board of transport commissioners to intervene without delay with the C.P.R. and have the company reconsider its decision to cut to three trains per week its service between Montreal and Mont Laurier and to operate fewer trains between Ottawa and Montreal, on the north shore of the Ottawa river, that is on the Quebec side?
Such a change will be highly prejudicial to workers, students and business people in general.
Second, could the minister not convince the government that it would be better to give a grant to the C.P.R., if necessary, so as not to imperil any further the economy of my riding which is already considered as a designated area?
9020	HOUSE OF
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
Mr. Speaker asked that this question be put on the order paper.
Without criticizing the Speaker's decision, I must point out that if any question ever was urgent, this one is. Indeed, the C.P.R. intends to put its new service into effect within a fortnight.
If topics such as these do not seem as dramatic as international matters, the fact remains that we, members of parliament, were elected in a given riding, by certain electors and that we are the only political voice in parliament when such problems are raised which are of deep concern to the people.
There is no need of a one hour discussion to make the house aware of the facts.
In the case of the Ottawa-Montreal line, the C.P.R. had two round trips on the Quebec shore.
Hundreds of workers used to take those trains to their work and back. Hundreds of students used that transportation to travel either to the capital city or to the metropolis. Hundreds of businessmen and travellers also used those facilities.
I might add that the area which is most affected, the one extending from Buckingham to Lachute, is an area where, because of the magnificent lakes and forests, the tourist industry is highly developed.
But it so happens that the C.P.R. has just cut the number of its trains by half. Why? For reasons of economy, of course, despite all the evidence to the contrary.
The situation is even worse in Mont Laurier where the C.P.R. has cut down its trains from Montreal to three a week.
Mont Laurier, Mr. Chairman, is a tourist's paradise.
What kind of a policy is this which allows a private company, enjoying privileges almost equal to those of a crown corporation, to operate a system as long as it is a good paying proposition and to discontinue its services the moment it cannot make enough profits?
After all, the C.P.R. operates a public service, and the board of transport commissioners must immediately try to prevent a hopeless situation.
As I pointed out last Friday, half of my constituency is a designated area.
It is useless to speak about an economic recovery when the government knowingly allows the economy to deteriorate.
I have received letters, telegrams, telephone calls and resolutions from municipal councils. I know that my colleagues from Terrebonne (Mr. Cadieux) and from Argenteuil-Deux-Montagnes (Mr. Drouin) have also received


some. I know that the Minister of Transport is aware of those things. Then, what is the government waiting for to act quickly before it is too late?
I am calling for immediate action on behalf of my constituents and those of neighbouring ridings.

speakeroldname: Hon. G. J. Mcllraiih (Acting Minister of Transport):
maintopic: TRANSPORTATION-QUEBEC-PROPOSED REDUCTION IN C.P.R. TRAIN SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company notified the board of transport commissioners on September 21, 1964, of their intention to discontinue certain passenger train services effective October 25, 1964. Notices to this effect were posted in all railway stations served by the trains affected. The changes involve a reduction in the existing service between Ottawa and Montreal via the north shore and between Montreal and Mont Laurier. The changes do not involve the complete abandonment of passenger train service on either of the runs and consequently the railway company is under no obligation to secure the approval of the board of transport commissioners before making adjustments.
Because of the volume and substance of objections filed with the board with respect to the Ottawa-Montreal service, the railway company was directed by the board on October 9 to continue the existing service, pending a hearing to determine whether the operation of such trains should be continued or be allowed to be discontinued.
Up to the present time only one complaint has reached the board with respect to the Montreal-Mont Laurier service. The C.P.R. is being requested to file a submission by way of answer to this complaint and in the meantime no action has been taken to interfere with the proposed reduction of passenger train service on this latter run.
I might add that the representations made by the hon. member who has just spoken have also been drawn to the board's attention. Following investigation of complaints arising from the changes, the board has authority to ask the railway company concerned to continue the service or, if the service has been discontinued, to restore the service if such action is considered necessary in the public interest.

Mr. Speaker, on Friday last I asked the Minister

Would the minister inform the house what action he has taken to deal with this latest and graphic example of the plundering of Canadian natural resources by our United States neighbours?
My question was based on an article that appeared in Maclean's magazine of October 17, which was brought to my attention by two or three people who are very interested in this subject, and as a person who has been a practising conservationist for over 50 years I said I would bring the matter to the attention of the minister. This article is rather disturbing. It is entitled: "How Wealthy Sportsmen Are Plundering Our Last Frontier". It goes on to say:
Right now, Tree river is the hottest spot in North America for the spare no expense angler. It's also the most fiercely abused. As such, it's a shameful symbol of what we're allowing to happen to our fastest growing Arctic industry.
The article is very interesting indeed and I wish to quote a paragraph or two which particularly concerned the people who brought this matter to my attention. On page 40 of the magazine I read the following:
Last June, Donald Snowden, then chief of northern affairs' industrial division, tried to rescue sport fishing in the territories from its own success. He called meetings in Edmonton, among camp operators, bush pilots and fisheries experts, to discuss conservation.
The article also contains these words:
How soon will time run out for the char in the Tree river? The fisheries research board said last spring that, the way things were going up till then, there would be no more char in the Tree by the end of next summer. And an anonymous northern affairs official reported to his superiors that unless some order and some restraint were introduced to sport fishing throughout the territories, "We can expect a peak of frantic, competitive development passing from area to area and from lake to lake and from river to river with little left in its wake except abandoned buildings and campsites."
There are other paragraphs in this article in a similar vein. In any event, after reading it through very carefully, Mr. Speaker, I am of the opinion that this is a question that should receive the serious consideration of the minister. I ask him these two particular questions: I presume that as a result of my questions on Friday he has read the article and made some inquiries. My questions are, first, is this article substantially correct in its outline of the situation to which I have referred? If so, what action is the minister

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a copy of the article here. As my hon. friend has said, it starts on page 19 and goes over to page 38. I want to remind him that this is a fish story. As is the case with most fish stories, a certain amount of exaggeration is traditional and even permissible. Since we are endeavouring to develop the tourist business in the Northwest Territories, I am not too sad about it. The article relates to one small area, the Tree river which is a river flowing into the Great Bear lake, an area of about 11,000 square miles. Due to the means of transport by which fishermen can go in, the fishing camps are concentrated. One of the camps sustains 55 anglers at a time, so there is a tendency to fish out that particular area.
Dealing with the Tree area, I want to assure the hon. member that this was brought to my attention last January when I was in the United States. I picked up a very beautiful piece of literature showing a number of United States citizens holding up large fish they had obtained from Great Slave lake. Across the bottom of it was written, "We guarantee you 300 pounds of fish a day." I took this matter up with my officers at once. I am assured by them that most of the things that are written here are now past tense, because the operators themselves are fully conscious of what this would mean to them in the end. They have gotten together. In addition, the R.C.M.P. have decided to reduce the take of char out of the Tree river down to two tons for their dogs. They have been taking more than this. I can assure the hon. member, therefore, we are aware of the situation.
The control of the fishery is in the hands of the fisheries department. The R.C.M.P. and our wardens, in these very remote areas are in control of the management of the resources. The article relates to one or two very localized areas. We think and hope there are many fishing areas on Great Bear lake and we look toward a tremendous increase in tourism in that area. I can assure my hon. friend that the article is a little bit overdone, but from our point of view probably designed to attract a large number of visitors next year. A number of Canadians of course are going in. This is expensive fishing. I believe it costs $760 or $900 round trip from Edmonton, with seven days of fishing. We are try-
